stem_md: Initially, on the lower left and right corner of a  $2018\times 2018$  board, there're two horses, red and blue, respectively.  $A$  and  $B$  alternatively play their turn,  $A$  start first. Each turn consist of moving their horse ( $A$ -red, and  $B$ -blue) by, simultaneously,  $20$  cells respect to one coordinate, and  $17$  cells respect to the other; while preserving the rule that the horse can't occupied the cell that ever occupied by any horses in the game. The player who can't make the move loss, who has the winning strategy?
solution_md:
Very difficult but nice problem, as my 499th post. The answer is  $B$  wins.
Consider a path from the lower right corner  $X$  to the lower left corner  $Y$ . By colouring the board into black and white like chessboard we know the number of grids in the path is even, suggest the Path is  $X=A_1\to B_1\to A_2\to B_2\to\cdots\to A_n\to B_n=Y.$ Here is the strategy of  $B:$  
- If  $B$  is on  $A_i,1\le i\le n,$  for the next step  $B$  walks to  $B_n.$
- If  $B$  is on  $B_i,1\le i\le n$  and the next turn  $A$  is on  $Y,$  then  $B$  walks to  $A_{n+1}.$
- If  $B$  is on  $B_i,1\le i\le n$  and the next turn  $A$  is not on  $Y,$  then  $B$  walks back to  $A_{n}.$

Note that by the colouring above,  $A$  and  $B$  can never walk to a same grid, we just need by the strategy  $B$  can always keep wlaking, until the game ends, and it wins.
We only need to prove the position of two horses will not occur twice, this is easily proved as if  $B$  went on the same position,  $A$  must have the position earlier than  $B.$  so we are done. $\Box$

stem_md: Suppose  $a_1,a_2, \dots$  is an infinite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers and  $p_1, p_2, \dots$  is a sequence of distinct primes such that  $p_n \mid a_n$  for all  $n \ge 1$ . It turned out that  $a_n-a_k=p_n-p_k$  for all  $n,k \ge 1$ . Prove that the sequence  $(a_n)_n$  consists only of prime numbers.
solution_md:
The equation implies that  $a_n - p_n = a_k - p_k$ , so  $a_n - p_n$  is constant over positive integers  $n$ . Let  $c$  be this constant. 

Claim:  $c = 0$ . 
Proof: If not, we have that  $p_n \mid c$  for all  $n$ , so  $(p_i)$  is bounded. But  $a_i = p_i + c$  must be bounded too, absurd since it is infinite and strictly increasing.  $\square$ Now, we have  $a_n = p_n$ , so the sequence  $(a_i)$  consists only of prime numbers.

stem_md: On the circle, 99 points are marked, dividing this circle into 99 equal arcs. Petya and Vasya play the game, taking turns.  Petya goes first; on his first move, he paints in red or blue any marked point. Then each player can paint on his own turn, in red or blue, any uncolored marked point adjacent to the already painted one. Vasya wins, if after painting all points there is an equilateral triangle, all three vertices of which are colored in the same color. Could Petya prevent him?
solution_md:
Nice problem! Solved with [**Mathnerd2007**](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/user/789182)
On the circle, 99 points are marked, dividing this circle into 99 equal arcs. Petya and Vasya play the game, taking turns. Petya goes first; on his first move, he paints in red or blue any marked point. Then each player can paint on his own turn, in red or blue, any uncolored marked point adjacent to the already painted one. Vasya wins, if after painting all points there is an equilateral triangle, all three vertices of which are colored in the same color. Could Petya prevent him?
Answer is **NO** i.e. Vasya will win no matter what. First 2 observations,**1**. The parity of Petya's moves are odd (i.e. Petya moves $1st,3rd,5th,.....$ ) and that of Vasya is even.**2**. The indices of the vertices of an equilateral triangle are of the form $K,K+33,K+66$ . We will show that we will get an equilateral triangle on the $98th$ move i.e. Vasya's $49th$ move. The Strategy is as follows, Consider the game after the $33rd$ move, say the coloured points(consecutive) are $(K,K+1,K+2,.....,K+32)$ and the next move is of Vasya's. On this move Vasya will colour point $(K+33)$ with the same colour as that of point $K$ .Then Vasya will play symmetrically with Petya i.e. if Petya colours $K+98$ (Indices taken modulo $99$ ) Vasya will colour $K+34$ with the same colour,i.e. if Petya colours $K+I(I>33)$ Vasya will just colour $K+132-I$ with the same colour. Now since the number of points between $K$ and $K+66$ and between $K+33$ and $K+66$ is $32$ ,note that on the $97th$ move Petya will have to colour $K+65/K+67$ if Vasya follows the aforementioned strategy . Thus on the $98th$ move Vasya will colour $K+66$ with the same colour as that of $K+33,K$ and get the equilateral triangle ( $K,K+33,K+66$ ).This concludes **OUR** Proof $\blacksquare$

The game reduces to a nim game where two players taking turns removing objects one at a time from two piles of odd size and the guy to remove the last item from both piles win.

We claim that Petya cannot prevent Vasya with the following strategy. Label the vertices  $a_1, \ldots, a_{99}$ . Note that  $a_i, a_{i+33 \mod{100}}, a_{i+66 \mod{99}}$  form an equilateral triangle. Thus there are  $33$  triangles in total. Note that for the first  $33$  moves, Petya and Vasya must color a vertex of all 33 equilateral triangles since they will color  $33$  consecutive vertices, so we can assume that they colored  $a_1, \ldots, a_{33}$ . It also doesn't matter which color they pick because Vasya will be trying to maintain the colorings while Petya will be trying to destroy them, so we can assume that all vertices were colored red.  Since  $33$  is odd, it will be Vasya's turn to color, Vasya can color  $a_{34}$ , then if he gets to color  $a_{67}$  he will win, so Petya mustn't color  $a_{68}$  or  $a_{66}$ . 

We will prove that Petya can't stop Vasya from coloring  $a_{67}$ . We split the rest of the vertices into two groups of size  $31$ ,  $S_1=\{a_{35}, \ldots, a_{65}\}, S_2=\{a_{69}, \ldots, a_{99}\}$ . If Petya chooses from  $S_1$  then Vasya chooses from  $S_2$ , if Petya chooses from  $S_2$  then Vasya chooses from  $S_1$ . WLOG suppose Petya and Vasya picked  $S_1, S_2$  respectively. From here on Vasya can just make the choice in whichever group Petya made the choice in on the previous turn. If they alternate in  $S_2$ , Vasya will make the last pick in  $S_2$ . If Petya ever makes another choice in  $S_1$  before Vasya then alternating in  $S_1$  would also mean Vasya makes the last pick. If Vasya follow the strategy outlined above, there is no way for him to make the move in  $S_1$  first, so no matter how Petya plays he will end up being forced to color one of  $a_{68}$  or  $a_{66}$  first, in which case Vasya can follow by coloring  $a_{67}$  red. stem_md: In a card game, each card is associated with a numerical value from 1 to 100, with each card beating less, with one exception: 1 beats 100. The player knows that 100 cards with different values lie in front of him. The dealer who knows the order of these cards can tell the player which card beats the other for any pair of cards he draws. Prove that the dealer can make one hundred such messages, so that after that the player can accurately determine the value of each card.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2018 Contests/2018 All-Russian Olympiad/1635131.json

candidates:
After considering this problem hard, I finally found the following. 

Let  $a_i$  be the card written  $i$ . The dealer write the following one hundred messages; $a_1$  beats  $a_{100}$ ,  $a_3$  beats  $a_1$ ,  $a_{100}$  beats  $a_3$ ,  $a_3$  beats  $a_2$ ,  $a_4$  beats  $a_3$ ,  $\ldots$ ,  $a_{99}$  beats  $a_{98}$ . 

Then, we show that only  $a_i=i$  for any  $i=1,2,\ldots,100$  is possible. 
Since the first three messages are "trilemma", two of  $a_1, a_{100}, a_3$  contains 1 and 100. 
But  $a_3$  is beaten by two others and beats two others, it cannot be 1 or 100. 
Thus,  $a_1=1, a_{100}=100$ . 
From other 97 messages,  $a_2, a_3, \ldots, a_{99}$  are sorted order and none of them are 1 or 100,

solution_md:
On the $n\times n$ checker board, several cells were marked in such a way that lower lefft ( $L$ ) and upper right( $R$ ) cells are not marked and that for any knight-tour from $L$ to $R$ , there is at least one marked cell. For which $n>3$ , is it possible that there always exists three consective cells going through diagonal for which at least two of them are marked?
**Solution.** The answer is $\boxed{n\in 3\mathbb N+1}.$ First we prove that all $n$ of the form $3k+1$ work. Call a colouring of the checkerboard *bad* if there are no three consecutive squares among a diagonal with more than $1$ black square. Call a knight tour *white* if there is no black squares in that knight tour.**Claim 1.** Let $n=3k+1.$ In an bad colouring of an $n\times n$ checkerboard, there exists a white knight tour.**Proof.** We proceed by strong induction on $k.$ The base case is trivial that is for $n=4$ , it is true. Now, consider a checkerboard of dimension $n=3k+1$ where $m>1.$ Assign coordinates to each cell of the checkerboard with $L=(1,1)$ and $R=(n,n).$ Consider the set of cells $A=\{(a,a)\mid a=3i+1,~1\le i\le k-1\},$ There can be two cases, either $A$ contains a white cell or not.**Case (i).** $A$ contains a white cell. Let the white cell be $(3j+1,3j+1).$ Now, consider the checkerboards determined by the set of corners $C_1=\{L=(1,1),(1,3j+1),(3j+1,1),(3j+1,3j+1)\}$ and $C_2=\{(3j+1,3j+1),(3j+1,n),(n,3j+1),(n,n)=R\}.$ By our induction hypothesis, since $(3j+1,3j+1)$ is white, we can move our knight from $L$ to $(3j+1,3j+1)$ considering $C_1$ , and then considering $C_2$ we can move our knight from $(3j+1,3j+1)$ to $R$ , completing a white knight tour. **Case (ii).** All the cells of $A$ are black. Note that the checkerboard is symmetric along the diagonal at this moment, also both of $(2,3)$ and $(3,2)$ can't be black. Without loss of generality assume that $(3,2)$ is white. We now divide the proof into two subcases that is whether the cell $(3k,3k-1)$ is black or white.**subcase (a).** The cell $(3k,3k-1)$ is white. In our first move, we move our knight from $L$ to $(3,2).$ Consider the **square** determined by the set of corners $C=\{(3,2),(3k,2),(3k,3k-1),(3,3k-1)\},$ we have $(3k,3k-1)$ is white, so using induction hypothesis, we can move our knight from $(3,2)$ to $(3k,3k-1)$ and then we can directly move it to $R$ from $(3k,3k-1)$ in exactly one move. **subcase (b).** The cell $(3k,3k-1)$ is black. Again, in our first move we move our knight to $(3,2)$ . Observe that $(5,3)$ is white since $(4,4)$ is black. So we move the knight to $(5,3),$ now, consider the $4\times 4$ checkerboard determined by the set of corners $S_1=\{(5,3),(8,3),(5,6),(8,6)\},$ note that $(8,6)$ is white as $(7,7)\in A$ is black, so using the induction basis, we can move our knight to $(8,6).$ Again consider the $4\times 4$ checkerboard determined by the set of corners $S_2=\{(8,6),(11,6),(8,9),(11,9)\},$ similarly, we can now move our knight to $(11,9),$ continuing in this way at some point our knight will reach $(3k-1,3k-3).$ Now, consider the $4\times 4$ checkerboard determined by the set of corners $T=\{(3k-1,3k-3),(3k-1,3k),(3k-4,3k-3),(3k-4,3k-1)\},$ observe that as $(3k-2,3k-2)\in A$ is black so $(3k-4,3k-3)$ is white, hence using induction basis we can move our knight to the cell $(3k-4,3k-3).$ Also note that by the initial assumption $(3k,3k-1)$ is black so $(3k-2,3k+1)$ is white, also since $(3k-2,3k-2)\in A$ therefore $(3k-3,3k-1)$ is white and as $(3k,3k-1)$ is black hence $(3k-1,3k)$ is white, so now we can execute the following sequence of moves, \[(3k-4,3k-3)\longrightarrow(3k-2,3k+1)\longrightarrow(3k-3,3k-1)\longrightarrow(3k-1,3k)\longrightarrow R\] And our induction is complete. $\square$ Observe that Claim 1 is enough to conclude that all $n=3k+1,~k\ge 1$ works. We now prove that other $n$ doesn't work. There can be two possibilities $n=3k$ or $3k+2,$ for now let $n=3k,$ in this case we colour the whole $(3h+2)^{\text{th}}$ row black for all $h=0,1,2,\ldots,k-1.$ Note that the second row from the top is coloured. Consider the following colouring example of a $9\times 9$ board where $O$ denotes black squares and $*$ denote the cells where the knight can go after several moves starting from $L$ without landing on black squares. Obviously, there can't be an $*$ in $R,$ as seen by the example below. It is not hard to see that this type of construction holds for all $n=3k.$ \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline & * & & * & & * & & * & R\tabularnewline \hline O & O & O & O & O & O & O & O &O\tabularnewline \hline * & & * & & * & & * & &*\tabularnewline \hline * & & * & & * & & * & &*\tabularnewline \hline O & O & O & O & O & O & O & O &O\tabularnewline \hline & * & & * & & * & & * &\tabularnewline \hline & * & & * & & * & & * &\tabularnewline \hline O & O & O & O & O & O & O & O &O\tabularnewline \hline L & & * & & * & & * & &* \tabularnewline \hline \end{tabular} Now, if $n=3k+2,$ we colour the whole $(3h)^{\text{th}}$ row black for all $h=1,2,\ldots,k.$ Note that the two top rows aren't coloured. Consider the following colouring example of a $8\times 8$ board. Obviously, there can't be an $*$ in $R,$ as seen by the example below. It is not hard to see that this type of construction holds for all $n=3k+2.$ \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline * & & * & & * & & * & R\tabularnewline \hline * & & * & & * & & * & \tabularnewline \hline O & O & O & O & O & O & O & O \tabularnewline \hline & * & & * & & * & & * \tabularnewline \hline & * & & * & & * & & *\tabularnewline \hline O & O & O & O & O & O & O & O \tabularnewline \hline *& & * & & * & & * & \tabularnewline \hline L & &* & & * & & *& \tabularnewline \hline \end{tabular} And we are done. $\blacksquare$

stem_md: The board used for playing a game consists of the left and right parts. In each part there are several fields and there’re several segments connecting two fields from different parts (all the fields are connected.) Initially, there is a violet counter on a field in the left part, and a purple counter on a field in the right part. Lyosha and Pasha alternatively play their turn, starting from Pasha, by moving their chip (Lyosha-violet, and Pasha-purple) over a segment to other field that has no chip. It’s prohibited to repeat a position twice, i.e. can’t move to position that already been occupied by some earlier turns in the game. A player losses if he can’t make a move. Is there a board and an initial positions of counters that Pasha has a winning strategy?
solution_md:
For the sake of sanity, I'll call the players  $A$  and  $B$ , with  $A$  going first, and their names interchangeable with their respective chips. For further disambiguation,  $A$  is female, and  $B$  is male. I'll let the board be a graph  $G$ , with two parts  $X$  and  $Y$ , such that  $A$  begins in  $X$  and  $B$  begins in  $Y$ . Call the vertex  $A$  starts on  $A_0$ .

First, some basic facts. Note that after the  $t$ th move by  $A$ , both  $A$  and  $B$  are in  $X$  iff  $t$  is even, and otherwise  $A$  and  $B$  are both in  $Y$ . Similarly, after the  $t$ th move by  $B$ ,  $A$  is in  $X$  and  $B$  is in  $Y$  iff  $t$  is even, otherwise,  $A$  is in  $Y$  and  $B$  is in  $X$ . This implies that, before  $B$ 's move, both chips are in the same part. Hence, the only constraint on  $B$ 's move is that he cannot create a position that has previously occurred.

Now we claim that  $B$  always wins with the following strategy:  $B$  considers a path from his starting location to  $A_0$ .  $B$  will move back to the position he was in in before his last move, unless he's not allowed to, in which case he advances along the path. Note that he always advances or retreats one step along the path.

First -  $B$  cannot retreat twice consecutively, if he's following the strategy. After retreating once, both options given in the strategy instruct him to advance. Hence, once  $B$  reaches any point along the path, he cannot ever return to any point at least  $2$  steps back from it.

Next -  $B$  can always advance along the path. Suppose it's been true up to some point. This point will be the present.

If the destination has yet to be occupied by  $B$  at any previous point, no position with  $B$  occupying that point could have existed, so  $B$  is free to move there. 

Otherwise, that means that at some previous point,  $B$  has been at the destination - the point ahead of his current location along the path, and  $A$  was in the position that she's currently at, right after her move. If we go back to that previous instance of the position and consider  $B$ 's move immediately preceding it (it must have been  $B$ 's move due to the 'basic fact' above), it must have been an advance. Were it a retreat,  $B$  would have been retreating from a position two steps ahead of the position he's currently at, a contradiction to the first fact. But the position immediately preceding the advance is equivalent to the position at present time, right after  $A$ 's move, so  $A$ 's move just before the present time was illegal.

Now we've shown that the strategy is well-defined, and the move suggested is legal, up till the point where  $B$  has reached the end of the path, and is forced to advance. We'll eventually show that this cannot occur. Note that the moves  $B$  makes can be partitioned into chunks (which I'll call 'cycles') consisting several (possibly  $0$ ) pairs of advances and retreats, followed by 2 advances.

Within a cycle,  $A$  may not return to any vertex she's previously been in, except for the vertex she was in when the cycle began. Suppose otherwise, and consider the position just after she does so.  $B$  will have been alternating between two vertices, one in  $X$ , and one in  $Y$  (let's call these  $x$  and  $y$ ). Consider the previous time  $A$  was in the vertex she's currently in ( $n$ ), specifically the position just before  $B$ 's move.  $A$  would have been in  $n$ , and  $B$  would be in whichever of  $x$  and  $y$  are in the same part as  $n$ , preparing to move to the other. This is the same position as in present time, hence  $A$ 's move was illegal. The reason why it's possible if  $A$  moved back to the starting vertex is because in that case,  $B$  would have been in a vertex from the previous cycle instead of  $y$ , as would be the case with other vertices in the part.

Thus,  $A$  can only return to a vertex she's previously been in within a cycle, if that vertex is the vertex she began the cycle in. Since the two vertices  $B$  alternates between during a cycle are unique to that cycle, the only way a position is repeated, and  $B$  is forced to advance is if  $A$  returns to the starting vertex. Hence,  $A$  always starts a cycle on the same vertex,  $A_0$ .

Now consider the final cycle, the cycle where  $B$  alternates between  $A_0$ , and the vertex just before that on the path. Every time  $A$  moves into a vertex in  $Y$ ,  $B$  moves to  $A_0$ . Hence,  $A$  can never return to  $A_0$ , as it'll always be occupied by  $B$  when she moves into  $Y$ . Thus, she has to keep visiting new vertices indefinitely, which is impossible.

stem_md:
How many ordered pairs of real numbers  $(x,y)$  satisfy the following system of equations?
\begin{align*}x+3y&=3 \big||x|-|y|\big|&=1\end{align*} $\textbf{(A) } 1 \qquad 
\textbf{(B) } 2 \qquad 
\textbf{(C) } 3 \qquad 
\textbf{(D) } 4 \qquad 
\textbf{(E) } 8 $
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Rewrite  $x$  as  $3-3y$ . Thus, we have  $||3y-3|-|y||=1$ . 

If  $y\ge0$  and  $3y-3\ge0$ , we have  $|2y-3|=1$ , which gives the solutions  $(-3,2)$  and  $(0,1)$ . 

If  $y\ge0$  and  $3y-3\le0$ , we have  $|3-4y|=1$ , which gives the solutions  $(1.5,0.5)$  and  $(0,1)$ . 

If  $y\le0$  and  $3y-3\ge0$ , we have  $|4y-3|=1$ , which gives the same solutions as above. 

If  $y\le0$  and  $3y-3\le0$ , we have  $|3-2y|=1$ , which gives the solutions  $(-3,2)$  and  $(0,1)$ . 


Thus, the only solutions are  $(-3,2), (1.5,0.5),$  and  $(0,1)$ .  $\boxed{C}$ .</details>

Misplaced :P (it took me 5 min for this problem since I heron bash to find CG but it turned out that was useless :P) Anyway, by angle bisector we have $\frac{10}{50}=\frac{CG}{GB}=\frac{1}{5},$ so we can let $CG=x,$ and $GB=5x,$ so $[ABG]=\frac{GB+CG}{BC}\cdot 120=\frac{5}{6}\cdot 120=100$ and since $\triangle AFD,$ is similar to $\triangle AGB,$ with ratio $\frac{1}{2},$ the ratio of areas is $\frac{1}{4},$ so $[AFD]=25,$ hence $[FDBG]=100-25=\boxed{75}$

I'm useless at geometry so vector bash: place an origin at A and let vector AC = p, vector AD = q, so |p| = 10, |q| = 50. By the area condition, 1/2*|p x q| = 120, so |p x q| = 240. Also by definition, AD = 1/2q, AE = 1/2p. Now using the [vector equation for an angle bisector](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Angle_Bisector_Vector), the bisector has equation r = |p|q + |q|p = 10q + 50p, but this is just 10(5p + q), so to make the arithmetic simpler, we can just take it as r = x(5p+q). The equation of DE is r= 1/2p + y(1/2q - 1/2p) = (1/2 - 1/2y)p + 1/2yq, so equating p and q coefficients gives that at F, 1/2-1/2y=5x, 1/2y=x, so we can solve to get the position vector of F as 5/12p + 1/12q. We can find the position vector of G analogously as 5/6p + 1/6q. Now using the cross-product formula for triangle area, and basic properties of cross-product (distributive, anticommutative, a vector cross itself is zero), we get area of triangle FDB = 5/48*|p x q| and area of triangle BGF = 5/24*|p x q|, so area of FDBG = (5/48 + 5/24)*|p x q| = 5/16*|p x q| = 5/16*240 = 5*15 = 75, as required.

stem_md: For a positive integer  $n$  and nonzero digits  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$ , let  $A_n$  be the  $n$ -digit integer each of whose digits is equal to  $a$ ; let  $B_n$  be the  $n$ -digit integer each of whose digits is equal to  $b$ , and let  $C_n$  be the  $2n$ -digit (not  $n$ -digit) integer each of whose digits is equal to  $c$ . What is the greatest possible value of  $a + b + c$  for which there are at least two values of  $n$  such that  $C_n - B_n = A_n^2$ ? $\textbf{(A)} \text{ 12} \qquad \textbf{(B)} \text{ 14} \qquad \textbf{(C)} \text{ 16} \qquad \textbf{(D)} \text{ 18} \qquad \textbf{(E)} \text{ 20}$
solution_md:
Fairly easy for a 12 #25. Also easier than many 10 #25s imo; AMC 10 2015A #25 comes to mind.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Observe  $A_n = a(1 + 10 + \dots + 10^{n - 1}) = a \cdot \tfrac{10^n - 1}{9}$ ; similarly  $B_n = b \cdot \tfrac{10^n - 1}{9}$  and  $C_n = c \cdot \tfrac{10^{2n} - 1}{9}$ . The relation  $C_n - B_n = A_n^2$  rewrites as
\[c \cdot \frac{10^{2n} - 1}{9} - b \cdot \frac{10^n - 1}{9} = a^2 \cdot \left(\frac{10^n - 1}{9}\right)^2.\]
Since  $n > 0$ ,  $10^n > 1$  and we may cancel out a factor of  $\tfrac{10^n - 1}{9}$  to obtain
\[c \cdot (10^n + 1) - b = a^2 \cdot \frac{10^n - 1}{9}.\]
This is a linear equation in  $10^n$ . Thus, if two distinct values of  $n$  satisfy it, then all values of  $n$  will. Matching coefficients, we need
\[c = \frac{a^2}{9} \quad \text{and} \quad c - b = -\frac{a^2}{9} \implies b = \frac{2a^2}{9}.\]
To maximize  $a + b + c = a + \tfrac{a^2}{3}$ , we need to maximize  $a$ . Since  $b$  and  $c$  must be integers,  $a$  must be a multiple of 3. If  $a = 9$  then  $b$  exceeds 9. However, if  $a = 6$  then  $b = 8$  and  $c = 4$  for an answer of  $\boxed{\textbf{(D)} \text{ 18}}$ .</details>

<details><summary>Solution 25 (really cool problem!)</summary>So we have   $$ c\cdot \dfrac{10^{2n}-1}{9}-b\cdot \dfrac{10^n-1}{9}=\left(a\cdot \dfrac{10^n-1}{9}\right). $$  Expanding and clearing denominators we have obtain   $$ 9((c\cdot (10^{2n}-1)-b\cdot(10^n-1))=a^2(10^{2n}-2\cdot 10^n+1). $$  Moving terms to one side we get    $$ 10^{2n}(9c-a^2)+10^n(9b-2a^2)+1(9(b-c)-a^2)=0 $$  .  This means that for more than one  $n$  to work we must have  $9c=a^2$  and  $9b=2a^2$  (if these are satisfied then so is the last one).  We have  $b=2c$  and  $c$  is a perfect square, which gives the solutions  $(3,2,1),~(6,8,4)\implies \boxed{\text{(D)}~18}$ .

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Write  $A_n=a\left(\frac{10^n-1}{9}\right),B_n=b\left(\frac{10^n-1}{9}\right),C_n=c\left(\frac{10^{2n}-1}{9}\right)$ , so the equation boils down to \[c\left(10^n+1\right)-b=a^2\left(\frac{10^n-1}{9}\right).\] If  $n=1$ , this reduces to  $11c-b=a^2$ , which we can see has the solutions  $\left(2,7,1,1\right),\left(3,2,1,1\right),\left(4,6,2,1\right),\left(5,8,3,1\right),\left(6,8,4,1\right),\left(7,6,5,1\right),\left(8,2,6,1\right),\left(9,7,8,1\right)$ . Otherwise, assume  $n>1$ .

Now observe that the LHS is between  $c\left(10^n+1\right)-1=c00\ldots0\left(c-1\right)$  and  $c\left(10^n+1\right)-9=\left(c-1\right)99\ldots9\left(c+1\right)$  inclusive. Thus, we need the middle digit of  $a^2\left(\frac{10^n-1}{9}\right)$  to be either  $0$  or  $9$ . We can check to see that this happens when  $a=3,6,9$  to give the triples  $\left(3,2,1,n\right),\left(6,8,4,n\right)$  ( $a=9$  ends up having a unit digit which is unreachable).

Thus, the only values of  $a+b+c$  which give multiple values of  $n$  are  $6$  and  $\boxed{18}$ .</details>

<details><summary>Not smart solution</summary>If  $a=9$ ,  $c=8$ , which can't work because  $99^2>8888$  (and  $\frac{A_n^2}{10^{2n}}$  is strictly increasing, so we can just check  $n=2$ ).
If  $a=8$ ,  $c=6$ , which can't work because  $88^2>6666$ .
If  $a=7$ ,  $c=5$ , which can't work because  $77^2>5555$ .
If  $a=6$ ,  $c=4$ , and  $b=8$ , which does work (for at least two values) since  $4444-88=66^2$ . $b\le9$ , and  $a\le5\implies c\le3$ , so all other solutions have  $a+b+c\le17$ , meaning the above solution, with  $a+b+c=18$ , is optimal.</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $A_n=\frac{10^n-1}{9}a$ ,  $B_n=\frac{10^n-1}{9}b$ , and  $C_n=\frac{10^{2n}-1}{9}c$ .

\[\frac{10^{2n}-1}{9}c-\frac{10^n-1}{9}b=\frac{10^n-1}{9}\cdot\frac{10^n-1}{9}a^2.\]

We can divide out that common factor since it's not equal to zero, to obtain:

\[(10^n+1)c-b=\frac{10^n-1}{9}a^2.\]

This rearranges to:

\[10^n=\frac{b-c-a^2/9}{c-a^2/9}\]

Since we are given that there are two possible values of  $n$  that work for fixed  $a,b,c$ , we must have divided by zero, so  $c=\frac{a^{2}}{9}$ . Testing,  $a=9,c=9$  doesn't work.  $a=6, c=4$  does work, if  $b=8$ , then we have  $4444-88=4356=66^2$  and  $44-8=36=6^2$ . Thus, the wanted value is  $4+6+8=\boxed{18}\rightarrow\boxed{D}$ .</details>

We rewrite \[A_n=a(10^0+10^1+10^2+\ldots+10^{n-1})=a\cdot\frac{10^n-1}{9}, B_n=b\cdot\frac{10^n-1}{9}, C_n=c(10^0+10^1+\ldots+10^{2n-1})=c\cdot\frac{10^{2n}-1}{9}\]

Now we need \[c\cdot\frac{10^{2n}-1}{9}-b\cdot\frac{10^n-1}{9}=a^2\cdot(\frac{10^n-1}{9})^2\]

Divide both sides by  $\frac{10^n-1}{9}$ : \[c\cdot(10^n+1)-b=a^2\cdot\frac{10^n-1}{9}\]

We now set  $10^n=k$ . 

So \[c\cdot k+c-b=a^2\cdot \frac{k-1}{9}\implies 9ck+9c-9b=a^2k-a^2\implies (9c-a^2)k=9b-a^2-9c\implies k=\frac{9b-a^2-9c}{9c-a^2}\text{ or } 9c=a^2\]


If  $k=\frac{9b-a^2-9c}{9c-a^2}$ , then there is at most one possible value of  $n$ , a contradiction. So  $9c=a^2$ . 

Now we have  $c(k+1)-b=c(k-1)\implies b=2c$ .  $c$  is also a perfect square because  $9c$  is a perfect square. 

To maximize  $a+b+c$ , we need to maximize  $c$ , so  $a=6, b=8, c=4$ , which obviously works for  $n=1,2$ .  $\boxed{\textbf(D)\ 18}$ .

<details><summary>solution</summary>We have  $A=\underbrace{aa\cdots a}_{n\text{ digits}}=a(10^{n-1}+10^{n-2}+\dots+1)=a\cdot\frac{10^n-1}{9}$ , and similarly  $B=b\cdot\frac{10^n-1}{9}$  and  $C=c\cdot\frac{10^{2n}-1}{9}$ . We have
\[C_n-B_n=c\cdot\frac{10^{2n}-1}{9}-b\cdot\frac{10^n-1}{9}=A_n^2=a^2\cdot\frac{(10^n-1)^2}{9^2}.\] $n$  is a positive integer, so  $10^n-1>0$  and thus we may take out a factor of  $\frac{10^n-1}{9}$ , which gives
\[c(10^n+1)-b=\frac{a^2}{9}(10^n-1)\implies 10^n\left(\frac{a^2}{9}-c\right)=\frac{a^2}{9}-b+c.\]
If  $\frac{a^2}{9}-c$  and  $\frac{a^2}{9}-b+c$  were nonzero, then there would only be one solution for  $n$ , so we must have  $\frac{a^2}{9}=c=b-c$ . Hence  $a$  is a multiple of 3 and  $b=2c$ , so  $c\leq 4$ . We want to maximize the sum of digits, so  $a=6$  and thus  $c=4$ ,  $b=8$ , which gives  $a+b+c=6+8+4=\boxed{\textbf{(D)}\ 18}$ .</details>

Note that  $A_n$ ,  $B_n$ , and  $C_n$  are just repdigits, so we can easily find a closed form for them:

\[A_n = \frac{a}{9} (10^n-1),\]
\[B_n = \frac{b}{9} (10^n-1),\]
\[C_n = \frac{c}{9} (10^{2n}-1).\]

Rewrite the condition as  $C_n = A_n^2+B_n$  to get

\[\frac{c}{9} (10^{2n}-1) = \frac{a^2}{81} (10^n-1)^2 + \frac{b}{9} (10^n-1).\]

Dividing out a common factor yields

\[9c(10^n+1) = a^2(10^n-1)+9b\]
\[\implies (a^2-9c) \cdot 10^n = a^2-9b+9c\]
\[\implies 10^n = \frac{a^2+9b-9c}{a^2-9c}.\]

This can obviously produce at most one solution for  $n$  unless  $a^2 -9c = 0$ , at which point we have  $a^2+9b-9c = 0$  as well. Solving the system of equations yields  $a^2 = 9c$  and  $b = 2c$ , so we easily see that  $c = 4$  produces a maximal sum of  $\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 18}$ .

Which of the following describes the set of values of  $a$  for which the curves  $x^2+y^2=a^2$  and  $y=x^2-a$  in the real  $xy$ -plane intersect at exactly  $3$  points? $
\textbf{(A) }a=\frac14 \qquad
\textbf{(B) }\frac14 < a < \frac12 \qquad
\textbf{(C) }a>\frac14 \qquad
\textbf{(D) }a=\frac12 \qquad
\textbf{(E) }a>\frac12 \qquad
$
solution_md:
CalculusThe graphs are tangent at the point $(0,-a)$ . So there are basically two possibilities. There can either be one intersection if the parabola is less concave than the circle at this vertex, or three intersections if the parabola is more concave. stem_md:
How many nonnegative integers can be written in the form   $$ a_7\cdot3^7+a_6\cdot3^6+a_5\cdot3^5+a_4\cdot3^4+a_3\cdot3^3+a_2\cdot3^2+a_1\cdot3^1+a_0\cdot3^0, $$  where  $a_i\in \{-1,0,1\}$  for  $0\le i \le 7$ ? $\textbf{(A) } 512 \qquad 
\textbf{(B) } 729 \qquad 
\textbf{(C) } 1094 \qquad 
\textbf{(D) } 3281 \qquad 
\textbf{(E) } 59,048 $
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>With  $7$  replaced by an arbitrary nonnegative integer  $n$ , let  $c_n$  denote the number of possibilities. Clearly  $c_0=2$  ( $a_0=-1$  doesn't work).

First, note that all  $3^{n+1}$  choices of  $a_i$  lead to distinct integers. Indeed, suppose that two different choices of  $a_i$  gave the same integer, let them be  $a_i$  and  $b_i$ . Let  $j$  be the largest index in which  $a_j$  and  $b_j$  differ and WLOG let  $a_j>b_j$ . Then subtracting the representation with  $b_i$  from that with  $a_i$  gives the sum \[\left(a_j-b_j\right)3^j+\left(a_{j-1}-b_{j-1}\right)3^{j-1}+\ldots+\left(a_0-b_0\right)3^0.\] But the terms from  $0$  to  $j-1$  sum up to a number that is at least \[-2\left(3^{j-1}+\ldots+3^0\right)=-3^j+1,\] so the whole sum is at least  $1$ , contradiction.

Now, consider how to count the possibilities where the sum runs up to  $3^{n+1}$ . If  $a_{n+1}=-1$ , then the best that the other terms can add up to is  $\frac{3^{n+1}-1}{2}$ , so the number is negative. If  $a_{n+1}=0$ , then we reduce to the case for  $n$ , and there are  $c_n$  values here. If  $a_{n+1}=1$ , then the worst that the other terms can add up to is  $-\frac{3^{n+1}-1}{2}$ , so the number is always positive. There are  $3^{n+1}$  choices here. Thus, we have the recurrence relation \[c_{n+1}=c_n+3^{n+1}.\] With  $c_0=2$ , this can directly be solved to get that  $c_n=\frac{3^{n+1}+1}{2}$ , so with  $n=7$  we get  $\boxed{3281}$  possibilities.</details>

$
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>The triangle is a right triangle with side lengths  $20,21,$  and  $29$ . While your critiques are certainly valid - it's definitely the case that some of the geometry was not great - I think you're being too strict with your definition of "clever".  Keep in mind that different problems are "nice" to people of different skill levels, and so what might be obvious to you (someone who has had math contest training before!) might not be obvious to the vast majority of AMC contestants.  For example, let's consider my geometry #15, since that's a problem I'm quite familiar with.  In that problem, said similar triangles are not immediately apparent (in fact most of the edges and vertices of these two triangles don't appear in the accompanying diagram!), and contestants have to add them in themselves.  I would argue that those who are not as experienced in geometry might take a while to come up with the auxiliary lines necessary to construct the similar triangles.  Sure, this may not exactly be revolutionary stuff, but it's a tad bit above what one might find in a standard high school geometry class - and this is exactly what a early-mid AMC problem should be like.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Note that the altitude from B to AC has the least length. It has length  $\frac{420}{29}$  which is between  $14$  and  $15$ . Thus, the lengths from  $20$  to  $15$  are attainable on one side, and the lengths from  $21$  to  $15$  are attainable on the other side, which are  $\boxed{13}\rightarrow\boxed{D}$  lengths total.</details>

The shortest length would be the length of the altitude from  $B$  to  $AC$ . Suppose the altitude has length  $x$ . Then by similar triangles,  $x=\frac{20\cdot21}{29}=\frac{420}{29}$ . 

Since  $14<\frac{420}{29}<15$ , the shortest possible integer length can be  $15$ . The longest possible integer length is  $21$ . 

Note that each length except  $21$  is counted twice, which gives an answer of  $6\cdot2+1=\boxed{\textbf(D)\ 13}$ .

stem_md: Let  $a, b, c,$  and  $d$  be positive integers such that  $\gcd(a, b)=24$ ,  $\gcd(b, c)=36$ ,  $\gcd(c, d)=54$ , and  $70<\gcd(d, a)<100$ . Which of the following must be a divisor of  $a$ ? $\textbf{(A)} \text{ 5} \qquad \textbf{(B)} \text{ 7} \qquad \textbf{(C)} \text{ 11} \qquad \textbf{(D)} \text{ 13} \qquad \textbf{(E)} \text{ 17}$
solution_md:
Great problem
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Obviously, we know
\begin{align*}
\gcd(a,b) &= 24 = 2^3 \cdot 3 
\gcd(b,c) &= 36 = 2^2 \cdot 3^2 
\gcd(c,d) &= 54 = 2 \cdot 3^3 
70 < \gcd&(a,d)<100
\end{align*}
Then
\begin{align*}
a=2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot a_1 = 24 a_1 
b=2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot b_1 = 72b_1 
c=2^2 \cdot 3^3 \cdot c_1 = 108c_1 
d=2 \cdot 3^3 \cdot d_1 = 54d_1
\end{align*}
Therefore
\begin{align*}
\gcd(a,d)=2 \cdot &3 \cdot n=6n 
70<6&n<100 
12 \le &n \le 16
\end{align*}
Thus,
\begin{tabular}{c|c|c} $n$  &  $\gcd(a,d)$  & Implies  \hline $12$  &  $72=2^3 \cdot 3^2$  &  $3|a_1, 4|d_1$   $13$  &  $78=2 \cdot 3 \cdot 13$  &  $13|a_1, 13|d_1$   $14$  &  $84=2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7$  &  $7|a_1, 14|d_1$   $15$  &  $90=2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5$  &  $15|a_1$   $16$  &  $96=2^5 \cdot 3$  &  $16|d_1$  
\end{tabular}
When  $n=12$ ,  $\gcd(a,b) \ge 72$ , therefore this doesn't work. When  $n=14$ , the  $\gcd(c,d) \ge 108$ , which also doesn't work. When  $n=15$ , the  $\gcd(a,b) \ge 72$ , whoch doesn't work. Finally, when  $n=16$ , the  $\gcd(c,d) \ge 108$ . Therefore, this doesn't work either, leaving us with  $n=\boxed{13}$  which works.</details>

<details><summary>hmm</summary>Let  $2^{96}=x$  and  $3^{96}=y$ . Thus, we get  $\frac{81x+16y}{x+y}=z$ , for some number  $z$ . We then multiply both sides by  $x+y$  to get rid of the fraction, resulting in  $81x+16y=zx+zy$ . Subtracting  $zx$  and subtracting  $16y$  from both sides, we get  $81x-zx=zy-16y$ . Finally, we factor to get  $x(81-z)=y(z-16)$ . We divide by  $y$  and divide by  $81-z$  to get  $\frac{x}{y}=\frac{z-16}{81-z}$ . We know that  $\frac{x}{y}$  is between  $0$  and  $1$ , so  $z$  must be in the interval  $(16, 81)$ . The only such answer choice is  $\boxed{\textbf{(A)} 80}$</details>

stem_md: Sangho uploaded a video to a website where viewers can vote that they like or dislike a video. Each video begins with a score of 0, and the score increases by 1 for each like vote and decreases by 1 for each dislike vote. At one point Sangho saw that his video had a score of 90, and that  $65\%$  of the votes cast on his video were like votes. How many votes had been cast on Sangho's video at that point? $\textbf{(A) }   200   \qquad        \textbf{(B) }   300   \qquad    \textbf{(C) }   400   \qquad   \textbf{(D) }  500  \qquad  \textbf{(E) }   600 $

Note that $0.65x$ denotes the number of individuals who upvoted the video while $x - 0.65x = 0.35x$ denotes the number who downvoted; these in turn are the number of upvotes and downvotes the video received respectively. The key is to recognize the part of the problem statement which reads
Each video begins with a score of 0, and the score increases by 1 for each like vote and decreases by 1 for each dislike vote.
Hence the total score at the end of it all is equal to the number of upvotes minus the number of downvotes. This equals $0.65x - 0.35x$ , which simplifies to $0.3x$ . The motivation for this solution is pretty straightforward: we don't know what the value of $x$ is, we want to find it, and it should make sense that the total score should be related to this value of $x$ in some form. So let's set it equal to a variable! (Alternatively, remark that the fact that you can check each of the answer choices one by one implies that you can perform this sequence of steps for an arbitrary number of viewers; thus, it makes sense to compute this arbitrary value and then reverse-engineer the value of $x$ .)

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Draw in the lines from the upper right corner of  $S$  to the two nonright vertices of the triangle. This splits the whole triangle into  $S$ , two smaller right triangles, and another triangle with the hypotenuse as a base. Let  $S$  have side length  $s$ , then the area of the square is  $s^2$ , the area of the smaller right triangles are  $\frac{s\left(4-s\right)}{2}$  and  $\frac{s\left(3-s\right)}{2}$ , and the area of the other triangle is  $\frac{5\cdot2}{2}=5$ . But the total area of the triangle is  $6$ , so we get the equation \[s^2+\frac{s\left(4-s\right)+s\left(3-s\right)}{2}+5=6.\] Solving this gives  $s=\frac{2}{7}$ , so the planted fraction is  $1-\frac{s^2}{6}=\boxed{\frac{145}{147}}$ .</details>

By similar triangles and ratios, the distance between the y-intercept of the new line and the y-intercept of the hypotenuse is  $3-\frac{5}{4} \cdot 2 = 3-\frac{5}{2}=\frac{1}{2}$ ; and our line has a slope of  $-\frac{3}{4}$  like the hypotenuse; so its equation is  $y=-\frac{3}{4}x+\frac{1}{2}$ .  The farthest corner of the square must lie on this line and  $y=x$ , thus it must be its intersection, which bashing gives is  $(\frac{2}{7}, \frac{2}{7})$ . These segments have length  $\sqrt{2s^2-6s+9}$  and  $\sqrt{2s^2-8s+16}$ .  Since the hypotenuse of the big triangle is  $5$ , we can find that  $\sqrt{2s^2-6s+5}+\sqrt{2s^2-8s+12}=5$ , so  $5-\sqrt{2s^2-6s+5}=\sqrt{2s^2-8s+12}$ . 

Squaring both sides gives \[2s^2-6s+30-10\sqrt{2s^2-6s+5}=2s^2-8s+12\], so  $2s+18=10\sqrt{2s^2-6s+5}$ . 

Squaring both sides again gives \[4s^2+72s+324=200s^2-600s+500\implies 196s^2-672s+176=0\implies 49s^2-168s+44=0\]. 

So  $49s^2-168s+44=(7s-2)(7s-22)=0\implies s=\frac{2}{7},\frac{22}{7}$ . Since  $\frac{22}{7}>3$  is an extraneous solution, we have  $s=\frac{2}{7}$ . 

The area of the big triangle is  $\frac{3\cdot4}{2}=6$ . Thus, the answer is \[1-\frac{s^2}{6}=1-\frac{4}{294}=\frac{290}{294}=\boxed{\textbf(D)\ \frac{145}{147}}\]</details>

stem_md: A unit of blood expires after  $10!=10\cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdots 1$  seconds. Yasin donates a unit of blood at noon of January 1. On what day does his unit of blood expire? $\textbf{(A) }\text{January 2}\qquad\textbf{(B) }\text{January 12}\qquad\textbf{(C) }\text{January 22}\qquad\textbf{(D) }\text{February 11}\qquad\textbf{(E) }\text{February 12}$
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>There are  $60$  seconds in a minute,  $60$  minutes in a hour, and  $24$  hours in a day. This means that Yasin's blood will expire after   $$ \frac{10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot\cdot\cdot2\cdot1}{60\cdot60\cdot24}= $$    $$ \frac{10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1}{60\cdot60\cdot24}= $$    $$ \frac{10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6\cdot5}{60\cdot60}= $$    $$ \frac{(10\cdot6)\cdot(9\cdot8\cdot5)\cdot7}{60\cdot60}= $$    $$ \frac{(360)(7)}{60}=6\cdot7=42. $$    $42$  days after January 1st is Feburary 12  $\Longrightarrow\boxed{\mathbf{(E)}}.$</details>

Note that there are \[60\cdot60\cdot24=3\cdot3\cdot4\cdot5\cdot6\cdot8\cdot10\] seconds in a day. 

We have \[\frac{10!}{3\cdot3\cdot4\cdot5\cdot6\cdot8\cdot10}=\frac{1\cdot2\cdot7\cdot9}{3}=2\cdot7\cdot3=42.\]

So  $10!$  seconds is  $42$  days.  Since January has  $31$  days,  $31$  days later is February  $1$ .  $42-31=11$  days after is  $\boxed{\textbf(E)\ \text{February 12 }}$ .

solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>If  $a=1$ , there would be no other numbers because  $a$  is divisible by every number.
If  $a=2$ , then you would include the prime numbers,  $(3,5,7,11)$ . You can’t add another number because it would either be divisible by  $2$ ,  $3$ , or  $5$ .
If  $a=3$ , then you would include  $(5,7,11)$  and the number  $4$  because there hasn’t been any even numbers. You can’t add anything else because it would be divisible by  $3$ ,  $4$ , or  $5$ .
If  $a=4$ , then you would include  $(5,7,11)$  and the numbers  $6$  and  $9$  because there is no  $3$ . Therefore  $\boxed{4}$  is our answer.</details>

solution_md:
When 7 fair standard 6-sided dice are thrown, the probability that the sum of the numbers on the top faces is 10 can be written as $$ \frac{n}{6^7}, $$ where $n$ is a positive integer. What is $n$ ? $\textbf{(A) } 42 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 49 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 56 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 63 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 84 $
I really should have used Stars and Bars for this problem. Except that I did not.
SolutionNotice that $n$ is the number of ways to roll seven fair dice that sum to $10$ . If the largest number is $5$ or more, there cannot be enough $1$ 's to add up to $10$ . Thus the largest number can be $2,3$ or $4$ . This is just casework on the number of ordered partitions of $10$ :**Case 1:**The largest number is $4$ . The distribution is $1+1+1+1+1+1+4$ , which gives $\binom{5}{1}=5$ cases.**Case 2:**The largest number is $3$ . The distribution is $3+2+1+1+1+1+1$ , which gives $\frac{7!}{5!}=42$ possibilities.**Case 3:**The largest number is $2$ . The distribution is $2+2+2+1+1+1+1$ , which is $\binom{7}{3}=35$ cases. We can confirm by hand that these are the only possibilities. Our final answer is $n=5+42+35=\boxed{84} \implies \boxed{\textbf{(E) }84}$

stem_md: How many ways can a student schedule 3 mathematics courses -- algebra, geometry, and number theory -- in a 6-period day if no two mathematics courses can be taken in consecutive periods? (What courses the student takes during the other 3 periods is of no concern here.) $\textbf{(A) }3\qquad\textbf{(B) }6\qquad\textbf{(C) }12\qquad\textbf{(D) }18\qquad\textbf{(E) }24$
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $A,G,$  and  $NT$  represent Algebra, Geometry, and Number Theory, respectively. Assume, WLOG that Algebra comes befoe Geometry, and Geometry comes before Number Theory. We will have to multiply our answer by  $3!=3\cdot2\cdot1=6$  at the end. The possible arrangements are   $$ \underline{A}\text{ }\underline{C}\text{ }\underline{G}\text{ }\underline{C}\text{ }\underline{NT}\text{ }\underline{C} $$    $$ \underline{A}\text{ }\underline{C}\text{ }\underline{G}\text{ }\underline{C}\text{ }\underline{C}\text{ }\underline{NT} $$    $$ \underline{A}\text{ }\underline{C}\text{ }\underline{C}\text{ }\underline{G}\text{ }\underline{C}\text{ }\underline{NT} $$    $$ \underline{C}\text{ }\underline{A}\text{ }\underline{C}\text{ }\underline{G}\text{ }\underline{C}\text{ }\underline{NT}, $$   where  $C$  represents a class that we don't know the name of. Thus, the answer is  $4\cdot6=24\Longrightarrow\boxed{\mathbf{(E)}}.$</details>

stem_md: Alice, Bob, and Charlie were on a hike and were wondering how far away the nearest town was. When Alice said, "We are at least 6 miles away," Bob replied, "We are at most 5 miles away." Charlie then remarked, "Actually the nearest town is at most 4 miles away." It turned out that none of the three statements were true. Let  $d$  be the distance in miles to the nearest town. Which of the following intervals is the set of all possible values of  $d$ ? $\textbf{(A) }   (0,4)   \qquad        \textbf{(B) }   (4,5)   \qquad    \textbf{(C) }   (4,6)   \qquad   \textbf{(D) }  (5,6)  \qquad  \textbf{(E) }   (5,\infty) $
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Alice's statement not being true means that they are less than  $6$  miles away. 

Bob's statement not being true means that they are more than  $5$  miles away. 

Charlie's statement not being true means they are more than  $4$  miles away.

Thus,  $d<6$  and  $d>5$ , which gives an answer of  $\boxed{D}$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2018 Contests/2018 AMC 10/1588287.json

candidates: This is also #4 on the AMC 12.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>The inequalities provided by Alice, Bob, and Charlie are  $d\geq6,d\leq5,d\leq4$ . Reversing each of these gives  $d<6,d>5,d>4$ . The intersection of these sets is  $\boxed{\left(5,6\right)}$ .</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>The three statements are  $d\geq6,d\leq5,$  and  $d\leq4.$  Since they are all false, the three statement  $d<6,d>5$  and  $d>4$  are true. This means that  $d\in(5,6)\Longrightarrow\boxed{\mathbf{(D)}}.$</details>

 Substituting the second equation into the first and third equation we have  $2a+c=20$  and  $3a+5c=58$ . Then  $5(2a+c)-(3a+5c) = 42 \implies c=6$ . Then we have  $a=8$  so the answer is  $8-6 = \boxed{2}$</details>

stem_md: Let  $ABCDEF$  be a regular hexagon with side length  $1$ . Denote by  $X, Y,$  and  $Z$  the midpoints of  $\overline{AB}$ ,  $\overline{CD}$ , and  $\overline{EF}$ , respectively. What is the area of the convex hexagon whose interior is the intersection of the interiors of  $\triangle ACE$  and  $\triangle XYZ$ ? $\textbf{(A) }\dfrac{3}{8}\sqrt{3}\qquad\textbf{(B) }\dfrac{7}{16}\sqrt{3}\qquad\textbf{(C) }\dfrac{15}{32}\sqrt{3}\qquad\textbf{(D) }\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{3}\qquad\textbf{(E) }\dfrac{9}{16}\sqrt{3}$
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Firstly, note that all six of the small triangles created by  $\triangle{XYZ}$  and  $\triangle{ABC}$  are congruent. Since  $Z$  is the midpoint of  $EF$ ,  $EZ=FZ=\frac{1}{2}$ . Drop an altitude from  $F$  to  $\overline{DE}$ . Let that intersection be  $L$ . Note that  $\triangle{FLE}$  is a  $30-60-90$  triangle. Drop an altitude from  $Z$  to  $EL$ , letting that intersection be  $M$ . The ratio of  $\triangle{ZME}$  to  $\triangle{FLE}$  is  $\frac{1}{2}$ , so  $ME=\frac{1}{4}$ . Let  $AE$  and  $ZY$  intersect at point  $N$ .  $ME=ZN$ , so  $ZY=\frac{3}{2}$ . Since  $\triangle{XYZ}$  is equilateral, its area is  $\frac{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2\sqrt3}{4}=\frac{9\sqrt3}{16}$ . The area of the hexagon created by the intersection between  $\triangle{ACE}$  and  $\triangle{XYZ}$  is just the area of one of those equilateral triangles minus the area of three of the small triangles mentioned earlier.  $[\text{Small triangle}]=[\triangle{ZME}]=\frac{\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{\sqrt3}{4}}{2}=\frac{\sqrt3}{32}$ .  $\frac{9\sqrt3}{16}-3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{32}=\boxed{\frac{15\sqrt3}{32}}$ .</details>

stem_md: Let  $\lfloor x\rfloor$  denote the greatest integer less than or equal to  $x$ .  How many real numbers  $x$  satisfy the equation  $x^2 + 10{,}000\lfloor x \rfloor = 10{,}000x$ ? $\textbf{(A) } 197 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 198 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 199 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 200 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 201$
solution_md:
SolutionLet $\lfloor x\rfloor = k$ and $x-k=\epsilon.$ Then this is $$ x^2 = 10000(x-\lfloor x \rfloor) \implies (k+\epsilon)^2 = 10000\epsilon \implies k^2 + 2\epsilon k + \epsilon^2-10000\epsilon $$ $$ \implies k=\frac{-2\epsilon \pm \sqrt{4\epsilon^2 - 4\epsilon^2 + 40000\epsilon}}{2} = \frac{-2\epsilon \pm 200\epsilon}{2} = \{99\epsilon,-101\epsilon\} $$ So since $k$ is an integer then $\epsilon$ is $\frac{a}{99}$ for $0 \leq a \leq 98$ or $\frac{b}{101}$ for an integer $0 \leq b \leq 100.$ In the former case since $k=99\epsilon$ we get $k=a$ so $x=a+\frac{a}{99} = \frac{100a}{99}$ for $a=0,1,\dots,98$ and the latter we similarly get $x=-b+\frac{b}{101} = -\frac{100b}{101}$ for $b=0,1,\dots, 100.$ The former case gave us only nonnegative $x$ and the latter only nonpositive so the only double-counted one is $0,$ so our total is $99+101-1 = \boxed{199}$

solution_md: <details><summary>solution</summary>[asy] pair A=(-12, 0), B=(12, 0), C=(-7.2, 9.6), O=(A+B)/2, G=(C+2O)/3; draw(circle(O, 12)); draw(circle(O, 4), blue); draw(A--B--C--cycle); draw(C--O, dashed); label(" $A$ ", A, W); label(" $B$ ", B, E); label(" $C$ ", C, dir(127)); label(" $G$ ", G, dir(53)); label(" $O$ ", O); [/asy] The centroid  $G$  of  $\triangle ABC$  is located two thirds of the way from  $C$  to the center  $O$  of the circle. Since the radius of the circle is  $12,$  it is always  $\displaystyle\frac{12}{3}=4$  units away from  $O$ . stem_md: A function  $f$  is defined recursively by  $f(1)=f(2)=1$  and   $$ f(n)=f(n-1)-f(n-2)+n $$   for all integers  $n \geq 3$ . What is  $f(2018)$ ? $\textbf{(A)} \text{ 2016} \qquad \textbf{(B)} \text{ 2017} \qquad \textbf{(C)} \text{ 2018} \qquad \textbf{(D)} \text{ 2019} \qquad \textbf{(E)} \text{ 2020}$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Define  $g(n)=f(n)-n$ . So  $g(n)+n=g(n-1)+n-1-g(n-2)-n+2+n=g(n-1)-g(n-2)+n+1$ , so  $g(n)=g(n-1)-g(n-2)+1$ . 


We also have  $g(1)=0$  and  $g(2)=-1$ . The pattern for  $g(n)$ , starting from  $n=1$  is: $0,-1,0,2,3,2,0,-1,\ldots$ . 

We see that the pattern repeats at  $n=7$ . So  $g(n)=g(n+6)$  for all positive integers  $n$ . Since  $2018\equiv2\pmod6$ , we have  $g(2018)=g(2)=-1$ . 

Thus,  $f(2018)=-1+2018=\boxed{(B)\ 2017}$ .</details>

This is equivalent to finding all integers  $m$  such that  $\tfrac{10^m+1}{10^2+1}$  is an integer. Now remark that  $10^2\equiv -1\pmod{101}$  but  $10^4\equiv 1\pmod{101}$ , so in fact  $\text{ord}_{10}(101) = 4$ .  Hence  $4\mid m - 2\Rightarrow m\equiv 2\pmod 4$ .

stem_md: How many subsets of  $\{2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9\}$  contain at least one prime number? $\textbf{(A)} \text{ 128} \qquad \textbf{(B)} \text{ 192} \qquad \textbf{(C)} \text{ 224} \qquad \textbf{(D)} \text{ 240} \qquad \textbf{(E)} \text{ 256}$
solution_md:
Claim: For, a set, with  $n,$  elements, the number of subsets, is  $2^n.$ Proof 1: 
Each, element, can be either, in the set, or out of the set, yielding,  $2$ , options, hence,  $2^n.$ Proof 2:
Induction. The base case, with  $1,$  element obviously holds. Now, if we have a set, with  $n,$  elements, and we add another element, we can choose the element, to be used, or to be taken out. In either, case we get  $2^n,$  options, hence,  $2^n+2^n=2^{n+1}.$ Now, the amount of subsets, using the claim, is  $2^8=256.$  Now, the amount of subsets, that contain no prime numbers, is  $2^4,$  hence,  $2^8-2^4=\boxed{240}.$

stem_md: Let  $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_{2018}$  be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers such that   $$ a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_{2018}=2018^{2018}. $$  What is the remainder when  $a_1^3+a_2^3+\cdots+a_{2018}^3$  is divided by  $6$ ? $\textbf{(A)}\ 0\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 1\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 2\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 3\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 4$
solution_md: <details><summary>oops most overkill solution</summary>Let  $a_1 = 1$ ,  $a_2 = 2$ ,  $\cdots$  for  $n = 1, \cdots 2017$ , and let  $a_{2018} = 2018^{2018} - \frac{(2017)(2018)}{2}$ . We want  $1^3 + 2^3 + \cdots + 2017^3 + (2018^{2018} - \frac{(2017)(2018)}{2})^3 \pmod 6$ , which is equivalent to  $(\frac{(2017)(2018)}{2})^2 + (2018^{2018} - \frac{(2017)(2018)}{2})^3 \pmod 6$ . Since  $1\equiv 2017 \pmod 6$  and  $2 \equiv 2018 \pmod 6$ ,  $2017 \cdot 2017 \pmod 6 \equiv 1 \cdot 2$ , so  $\frac{(2017)(2018)}{2} \equiv 1 \pmod 6$ . Notice that when we take powers of  $2018$ , they alternate between  $2$  and  $4$ , so  $2018^{2018} \pmod 6 \equiv 4$  since  $2018 \pmod 2 \equiv 2$ . Our answer is  $1^2 + (4-1)^3 \pmod 6 \equiv \boxed{4}$ .</details>

stem_md: Joey and Chloe and their daughter Zoe all have the same birthday. Joey is 1 year older than Chloe, and Zoe is exactly 1 year old today. Today is the first of the 9 birthdays on which Chloe's age will be an integral multiple of Zoe's age. What will be the sum of the two digits of Joey's age the next time his age is a multiple of Zoe's age? $\textbf{(A) } 7 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 8 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 9 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 10 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 11 $
solution_md:
Let Joey's age be $j$ , Chloe's age be $c$ , and we know that Zoe's age is $1$ . We know that there must be $9$ values $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $c+k=a(1+k)$ where $a$ is an integer. Therefore, $c-1+(1+k)=a(1+k)$ and $c-1=(1+k)(a-1)$ . Therefore, we know that, as there are $9$ solutions for $k$ , there must be $9$ solutions for $c-1$ . We know that this must be a perfect square. Testing perfect squares, we see that $c-1=36$ , so $c=37$ . Therefore, $j=38$ . Now, since $j-1=37$ , by similar logic, $37=(1+k)(a-1)$ , so $k=36$ and Joey will be $38+36=74$ and the sum of the digits is $\boxed{\text{(E) }11}$

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $J$ ,  $C$ , and  $Z$  denote the ages of the family members.  For Chloe's age to be an integral multiple of Zoe's age  $9$  times, their difference should have  $9$  divisors.  We have that  $C - Z$  has 9 divisors .  Zoe is  $1$  year old right now, so we can plug that in because the difference between the ages stay constant, so we have  $C - 1$  has 9 divisors.  We need to find the least positive integer that has  $9$  divisors to find the difference.  The minimum value is  $2^2 \cdot 3^2 = 36$ .   $36$  must be the difference of Chloe and Zoe's ages, so as of now, Zoe's age is  $1$ , and Chloe's age is  $37$ .  This means that Joey's age is  $38$ .  We want to find the next time that Joey's age is a multiple of Chloe's age.  Since the difference of Joey's age and Zoe's age is a prime number ( $37$ ), the next time that happens would be when Zoe's age is  $37$  and Joey's age is  $74$ .  Thus, our answer is  $7 + 4 = 11 \implies \boxed{\text{E}}$ .</details>

stem_md: Mary chose an even  $4$ -digit number  $n$ . She wrote down all the divisors of  $n$  in increasing order from left to right:  $1,2,...,\tfrac{n}{2},n$ . At some moment Mary wrote  $323$  as a divisor of  $n$ . What is the smallest possible value of the next divisor written to the right of  $323$ ? $\textbf{(A) } 324 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 330 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 340 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 361 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 646$
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Let the next divisor be  $k$ . Note that the smallest possible value of  $n$  is  $\operatorname{lcm}(2,323,k)$ . If  $\gcd(323,k) = 1$ , then  $n$  is at least  $323 \cdot  k > 9999$ . Hence,  $k$  must share a divisor with  $323 = 17 \cdot 19$ . The smallest multiple of  $17$  greater than  $323$  is  $340$ , and the smallest multiple of  $19$  greater than  $323$  is  $342$ . Taking  $k = 340$  gives  $n = 6460$ , which works, so our answer is  $\boxed{\textbf{(C) }340}$ .</details>

solution_md:
<details><summary>Note</summary>I thought for sure there was a trick to this one. Also, I had to do this one without scrap paper because my proctor had at this point neglected to give me any :what?:.</details>
<details><summary>Elementary Solution</summary>We are trying to convert from basis vectors of  $(1,0)$  and  $(0,1)$  to basis vectors of  $(2,0)$  and  $(0,2)$ . The matrix for doing so is
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{2} & 0
0 & \frac{1}{2}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The original cornbread was the parallelogram demarcated by the points  $(20,0)$  and  $(0,18)$ , so the new parallelogram consists of the vectors
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{2} & 0
0 & \frac{1}{2}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
20 & 0
0 & 18
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
10 & 0
0 & 9
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Since
\[ [2, 0] \cdot [0,2] = 0\] $(2,0)$  and  $(0,2)$  are orthonormal basis vectors and the area covered by the points  $(10,0)$  and  $(0,9)$  is 
the absolute value of
\[ \det\left(
\begin{bmatrix}
10 & 0
0 & 9
\end{bmatrix}
\right)
= 90
 \]
We draw this out on a number line and it is easy to see that  $90$  is  $90$  units away from  $0$ , so our answer is  $\boxed{90}$</details>

stem_md: How many ordered pairs  $(a, b)$  of positive integers satisfy the equation   $$ a\cdot b + 63 = 20\cdot \text{lcm}(a, b) + 12\cdot\text{gcd}(a,b), $$  where  $\text{gcd}(a,b)$  denotes the greatest common divisor of  $a$  and  $b$ , and  $\text{lcm}(a,b)$  denotes their least common multiple? $\textbf{(A)}\ 0\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 2\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 4\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 6\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 8$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $x=lcm(a,b)$  and let  $y=gcd(a,b)$ . So  $ab=xy$ . 

The equation is now  $xy+63=20x+12y$ , so  $xy-20x-12y+63=0$ . Note that  $(x-12)(y-20)=xy-20x-12y+240=240-63=177$ . 

We can either have  $x-12=59$  and  $y-20=3$ , or  $x-12=177$  and  $y-20=1$ . 

Since we can't have  $x=71, y=23$ , we must have  $x=189$  and  $y=21$ . 

We find that the only solutions here are  $(a,b)=(21,189)$  and  $(a,b)=(189,21)$ . So the answer is  $\boxed{B}$ .</details>

Let  $\overline{AB}=\overline{BC}=\overline{CD}=n$ . 
Since  $\overline{PQ}=8$ ,  $\overline{BQ}=\frac{8-n}{2}=4-0.5n$ , and similarly  $\overline{CQ}=3-0.5n$ . 
By the Pythagorean Theorem, 
\begin{align}
\nonumber \overline{BQ}^2+\overline{CQ}^2&=\overline{BC}^2
\nonumber (4-0.5n)^2+(3-0.5n)^2&=n^2
\nonumber (16-4n+0.25n^2)+(9-3n+0.25n^2)&=n^2
\nonumber 25-7n+0.5n^2&=n^2
\nonumber 0.5n^2+7n-25&=0
\nonumber n^2+14n-50&=0
\end{align}
Then complete the square, 
\begin{align}
\nonumber (n+7)^2&=99
\nonumber n+7&=\pm\sqrt{99}
\nonumber n&=-7\pm\sqrt{99}
\end{align}  $$ n=-7+3\sqrt{11}\;or\;n=-7-3\sqrt{11} $$  Since  $-7-3\sqrt{11}$  is negative,  $n=-7+3\sqrt{11}$ .  $k+m+n=-7+3+11=7$ , so the answer is  $\boxed{\text{(B)}~7}$  .</details>

stem_md: A box contains  $5$  chips, numbered  $1$ ,  $2$ ,  $3$ ,  $4$ , and  $5$ . Chips are drawn randomly one at a time without replacement until the sum of the values drawn exceeds  $4$ . What is the probability that  $3$  draws are required? $\textbf{(A)} \frac{1}{15} \qquad \textbf{(B)} \frac{1}{10} \qquad \textbf{(C)} \frac{1}{6} \qquad \textbf{(D)} \frac{1}{5} \qquad \textbf{(E)} \frac{1}{4}$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>If  $1$  is chosen, then you can choose  $2$  or  $3$  on the second move and the third move is guaranteed to exceed  $4$  either away, leaving us with  $\dfrac{1}{5}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{10}$ .

If  $2$  is chosen, you must choose  $1$  next or else you already exceed  $4$ , so this is  $\dfrac{1}{5}\cdot\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{1}{20}$ .

If  $3$  is chosen, then  $1$  must be chosen next for the same reason, so it's  $\dfrac{1}{5}\cdot\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{1}{20}$ .

Lastly,  $4$  and  $5$  cannot be chosen because it would already exceed 4.

Therefore our probability is  $\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{1}{20}+\dfrac{1}{20}=\boxed{\dfrac{1}{5}}$ .</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Alright, let's begin by assuming there are  $n$  semicircles, where  $n$  is a positive integer. Next, if the radius of each small semicircle is  $r$ , we get that the large radius is  $nr$ . Knowing that the ratio of the inside of semicircles to the outside of the semicircles is  $1:18$ , we have $\frac{1}{2}(nr)^2\pi-n(\frac{1}{2}r^2\pi)=18n(\frac{1}{2}r^2\pi)$ .

Dividing both sides by  $nr^2\pi$ , we have $\frac{1}{2}n-\frac{1}{2}=18(\frac{1}{2})=9$ .

Therefore,  $\frac{1}{2}n=9+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{19}{2}$ , so  $n=\boxed{19 (D)}$ .</details>

solution_md: <details><summary>My solution</summary>The lengths of the dashed lines are the height of the box, so the area of the square is the combined area of two corner triangles of the square (both of which have hypotenuse length  $2h+w$ , and thus leg length  $\frac{2h+w}{\sqrt{2}}$ ) and the area of the stuff in between, which is the area of the rectangle with length  $2h+w$  and width  $w$  added to the areas of two triangles with hypotenuse length  $w$  and thus leg length  $\frac{w}{\sqrt{2}}$ . Thus, the area of our square is   $$ \left(\frac{2h+w}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2+w(2h+w)+\left(\frac{w}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2=\frac{w^2+4h^2+4hw+w^2}{2}+2hw+w^2=2h^2+2hw+w^2+2hw+2w^2=2h^2+2hw+w^2=2(w+h)^2\implies\boxed{\mathbf{A}} $$</details>

solution_md:
**Motivation.** :D $J$ being the incenter of $\triangle MHN$ , along with $\overline{FJ}$ , appeals us to consider the Fact 5 thing of $FJ=FN=FM$ ; and further, as asked to prove $FJ=FA$ , $FN=FM$ appeals to show $F$ as the circumcenter of $\triangle AMN$ , so that we get $FA=FN=FM.$ [rule]
Let $H$ be the orthocenter of the triangle $ABC$ . Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$ , respectively. Assume that $H$ lies inside the quadrilateral $BMNC$ and that the circumcircles of triangles $BMH$ and $CNH$ are tangent to each other. The line through $H$ parallel to $BC$ intersects the circumcircles of the triangles $BMH$ and $CNH$ in the points $K$ and $L$ , respectively. Let $F$ be the intersection point of $MK$ and $NL$ and let $J$ be the incenter of triangle $MHN$ . Prove that $F J = F A$ .
[rule]**Solution:****Claim 1.** $F$ is the circumcenter of $\triangle AMN.$ *Proof.* We note that $$ 90^{\circ} - \angle A = \angle HBA = \angle HBM = \angle HKM = \angle NMF. $$ Similarly, $\angle MNF = 90^{\circ}-\angle A.$ So, $\angle MFN = 2\angle A$ , and thus, we get $F$ as the circumcenter of $\triangle AMN$ ; whence, $FA=FM=FN.$ **Claim 2.** $F$ is the midpoint of arc $MN$ , not containing $H.$ *Proof.* Let $\overline{HH}$ be the line through $H$ tangent to both $(HCN)$ and $(HMB).$ Now, due to Angles in Alternate Segment theorem, we have $$ \angle(\overline{HH},\overline{HN}) = \angle HCN = 90^{\circ} - \angle A = \angle HBM = \angle(\overline{HH},\overline{HM}). $$ This implies two things: firstly, that $\overline{HH} \equiv \overline{HJ}$ as it bisects the two angles which form $\angle MHN$ , and secondly, that $F\in(HMN)$ as $\angle MHN = 180^{\circ}-2\angle A$ , and $\angle MFN = 2\angle A$ from *Claim 1*. Now, as $\angle FMN = \angle FHN = 90^{\circ}-\angle A$ and $\angle JHN = 90^{\circ}-A$ , thus $F, J, H$ are collinear; indeed we have $FM=FN$ from *Claim 1*, and as $F\in(HMN)$ , therefore $F$ is the midpoint of arc $MN$ , not containing $H$ . And we're through with Fact 5. $\quad\blacksquare$

stem_md: Find all polynomials  $P(x)$  with integer coefficients such that for all real numbers  $s$  and  $t$ , if  $P(s)$  and  $P(t)$  are both integers, then  $P(st)$  is also an integer.
solution_md:
Assume that  $P$  is a non-constant solution. Let  $P(x) = a_d x^d + a_{d-1} x^{d-1} + \ldots + a_0$  (so  $a_d \neq 0$ ). Notice that if  $P$  is a solution, then so does  $Q\equiv -P$ , so WLOG assume  $a_d>0$ . We will use the following lemma.**Lemma 1**: For any polynomial  $Q\in\mathbb{R}[X]$  with degree  $d$  and leading coefficient  $a$ , and for any  $n>d$ ,   $$ \sum_{i=0}^d (-1)^{d-i} {d\choose i} Q(x+i) = d!a, \quad \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^{n-i} {n\choose i} Q(x+i) = 0 $$  *Proof*. Notice that  $\forall n\in\mathbb{N}$ , any polynomial of degree at most  $n$  is a solution of a recursive equation  $\sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^{n-i} {n\choose i} b_{k+i} = c$  for some real  $c$  and those of degree at most  $n-1$  is a solution at  $c=0$ . This means we have proved the second equality and for the first equality, we can pick  $Q(x)=d!a{x\choose d}$ . Also it becomes sufficient to only prove that  $\sum_{i=0}^d (-1)^{d-i} {d\choose i} {i\choose d} = 1$ . But this is trivial.**Lemma 2**:  $\boxed{\sum_{i=0}^d (-1)^{d-i} {d\choose i} P(xi) = d! a_d x^d}$ *Proof*. By lemma 1, for each  $0\leq n<d$ ,  $\sum_{i=0}^d (-1)^{d-i} {d\choose i} a_n (xi)^n=0$  and  $\sum_{i=0}^d (-1)^{d-i} {d\choose i} a_d (xi)^d = d! a_d x^d$ . Combining this completes our proof.**Lemma 3**: If  $t$  is a real number such that  $P(t)$  is an integer, then  $d! a_d t^d$  is an integer.

*Proof*. Since  $P(n)$  is an integer for every  $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ ,  $P(nt)$  is also an integer for every  $n \in \mathbb{Z}$  and thus using lemma 2, we get that  $d! a_d t^d$  is an integer.**Lemma 4**: If  $t$  is a real number such that  $P(t)$  is an integer, then  $t^d$  is an integer.

*Proof*. By induction,  $P(t^n)\in\mathbb{Z}$  for each  $n\geq 1$  and thus by lemma 3,  $d! a_d t^{nd}$  is an integer. By computing their p-adic valuation, we obtain that  $t^d$  is an integer.

Now, consider the continuous function  $f(x)=P(\sqrt[d]{x})=a_d x+\sum_{i=0}^{d-1} a_i x^{\frac{i}{d}}$  for  $x>0$ . By lemma 4,  $f(t)\in\mathbb{Z}$  implies  $t\in\mathbb{N}$ . Since  $f(x)\rightarrow \infty$  when  $x\rightarrow \infty$ , we can pick  $M$  big enough such that  $f(M)$  is an integer,  $f(x)$  is strictly increasing at  $x>M$  and  $f(x+2)-f(x)>1$  for every  $x>M$  ( $a_d\geq 1$ ). Let  $f(M)=M+c$ . By IVT, for each  $n\geq M$ , there exist  $x$  real such that  $n<x<n+2$  and  $f(x)$  is an integer, which means  $x=n+1$  and thus  $f(n)\in \mathbb{Z}$  for each  $n\geq M$ . But by IVT again,  $f(n+1)-f(n)=1$  and thus by induction  $f(n)=n+c \forall n\geq M$ .

Hence,  $P(x)=f(x^d)=x^d+c$  for infinitely many values of  $x$ , and thus  $P(x)=x^d+c$ . We're done.

Note: the solution  $P(x)=c$  works even if  $c$  is not an integer, but for  $P(x)=\pm x^d+c$ ,  $c$  is necessarily an integer. Hope the latex doesn't fail...

Define the polynomial $Q(z) = P( u z)$ . By the given condition, $Q(\mathbb{Z}) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ and thus by, say Polya all the coefficients of $Q$ are rational. In particular $ u^{\deg P} \in \mathbb{Q}$ . Write $k = u^{\deg P}$ . Since $x^{\deg P} - k$ is a polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}[X]$ with $ u$ as a root, it follows that $P$ , who is the minimal polynomial of $ u$ must divide this in $\mathbb{Q}[X]$ . But since they have the same degree, it follows that $P = K(x^{\deg P} - k)$ for some rational $K$ . All in all, we have that $P$ is of the form $ax^n+b$ for some integers $a, b$ and positive integer $n$ . Now we are done, since we may now switch $P$ for it's negative and translate it if necessary following which $P$ would take the form $ax^n$ for positive integers $a, n$ . Trivially, this gives $a = 1$ following which the solution set is: \[P \in \{t \in \{-1, 1\}, k \in \mathbb{Z} \mid tx^n+k\}\] all of which can be seen to work.

1 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0
1 & 1 & 1^2 & \dots & 1^n
1 & 2 & 2^2 & \dots & 2^n
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots

P(0)
P(x)
P(2x)
\vdots
P(nx)
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}
a_0
a_1x
a_2x^2
\vdots
a_nx^n\end{pmatrix}. $$  Furthermore, since the leftmost matrix has only integer entries, its inverse has only rational entries, and thus we get  $$ a_nx^n=\sum_{0\leq i\leq n}c_iP(ix), $$  for some rational numbers  $c_0,c_1,\dots,c_n$ . If $f$ is constant, then we are done, since $P(x) - k = f(x)g(x)$ is a trivial factorization (since $f$ is a unit in $\mathbb Z[x]$ ), so suppose $f$ is nonconstant. Then the product of the complex roots of $f$ has absolute value at most $1$ , so $P$ has some complex root inside the closed unit disk. Let  $f(x)$  and  $g(x)$  be given by  $f(x) = \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{x-2} + \frac{1}{x-4} + \cdots + \frac{1}{x-2018}$  $g(x) = \frac{1}{x-1} + \frac{1}{x-3} + \frac{1}{x-5} + \cdots + \frac{1}{x-2017}$ .

Prove that  $|f(x)-g(x)| >2$  for any non-integer real number  $x$  satisfying  $0 < x < 2018$ .
solution_md:
Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ be given by \[f(x) = \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{x-2} + \frac{1}{x-4} + \cdots + \frac{1}{x-2018}\] \[g(x) = \frac{1}{x-1} + \frac{1}{x-3} + \frac{1}{x-5} + \cdots + \frac{1}{x-2017}.\] Prove that $|f(x)-g(x)| >2$ for any non-integer real number $x$ satisfying $0 < x < 2018$ .
**Solution.** Define $h(x)=f(x)-g(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{2018}(-1)^i\frac{1}{x-i}.$ Note that $h(2018-x)=-h(x),$ so it suffices to check for the result for $x\in (0,1009).$ **Claim 1.** $-\frac{1}{x-(a-1)}+\frac{1}{x-a}+\frac{1}{(a+1)-x}-\frac1{(a+2)-x}>2$ for $x\in (a,a+1)$ where $a\in \mathbb N_0.$ **Proof.** Substitute $y=x-a,$ then $y\in(0,1)$ and we have to prove \[-\frac1{y+1}+\frac1{y}+\frac{1}{1-y}-\frac1{2-y}>2.\] Now, \begin{align*} -\frac1{y+1}+\frac1{y}+\frac{1}{1-y}-\frac1{2-y} &=\frac{1}{y(1-y)}-\frac3{(y+1)(2-y)} &=\frac{2y-y^2+2-y-3y+3y^2}{y(1-y)(y+1)(2-y)} &=\frac{2y^2-2y+2}{y(1-y)(y+1)(2-y)} &=2\cdot\frac{y^2-y+1}{y^4-2y^3-y^2+2y} \end{align*} Hence, it suffices to prove $y^2-y+1>y^4-2y^3-y^2+2y$ that is \[y^4-2y^3-2y^2+3y-1<0\] Taking derivatives, \begin{align*} \left(y^4-2y^3-2y^2+3y-1\right)'=4y^3-6y^2-4y+3 &=4y^2\left(y-\frac12\right)-4y\left(y-\frac12\right)-6\left(y-\frac12\right) &=2\left(y-\frac12\right)(2y^2-2y-3) &=2\left(y-\frac12\right)\underbrace{\left(2\left(y-\frac12\right)^2-\frac72\right)}_{-\text{ve}} \end{align*} Therefore, $y^4-2y^3-2y^2+3y-1$ is increasing in $\left(0,\tfrac12\right]$ and decreasing in $\left[\tfrac12,1\right).$ Thus, \[y^4-2y^3-2y^2+3y-1<\frac1{16}-\frac14-\frac12+\frac32-1=-\frac3{16}-1<0.\] Hence, the claim. $\square$ Coming back to the original problem, Let $x\in(a,a+1)$ where $a\in \mathbb N_0.$ We now divide the proceedings into two cases that is whether $a$ is even or odd.**Case (i).** $a$ is even. \begin{align*} stem_md:
A collection of  $n$  squares on the plane is called tri-connected if the following criteria are satisfied:

(i) All the squares are congruent.
(ii) If two squares have a point  $P$  in common, then  $P$  is a vertex of each of the squares.
(iii) Each square touches exactly three other squares.

How many positive integers  $n$  are there with  $2018\leq n \leq 3018$ , such that there exists a collection of  $n$  squares that is tri-connected?

Answer is all even numbers. We call a triple of squares which are pairwise touching a clover. Then touching two clovers at two points makes a joint. Putting five joints together in a regular pentagon makes a solution with  $30$ . We can also attach a square to one of the touching points of a clover so that the resulting figure has a line of symmetry and call it a hanging clover. Putting eight of these hanging clovers together gives a solution with  $32$ . By chicken nuggets this yields everything in the range that is even. If odd, double count incidences to finish.
The example is as beautiful as if the problem was created based on it.

stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be an equilateral triangle. From the vertex  $A$  we draw a ray towards the interior of the triangle such that the ray reaches one of the sides of the triangle. When the ray reaches a side, it then bounces off following the law of reflection, that is, if it arrives with a directed angle  $\alpha$ , it leaves with a directed angle  $180^{\circ}-\alpha$ . After  $n$  bounces, the ray returns to  $A$  without ever landing on any of the other two vertices. Find all possible values of  $n$ .

Each bounce corresponds to each time the line segment hits one of the reflected sides. These are just when the line segment hits one of the horizontal lines or any of the diagonal lines. Call the diagonals that go from top right to bottom left the ``RL diagonals'', and the ones that go from top left to bottom right the ``LR diagonals''. Also call the horizontal lines ``rows''. Suppose that the end vertex is in the  $y$ th row down and on the  $x$ th RL diagonal down (equivalently the  $\left(y+1-x\right)$ th LR diagonal down). Then the line segment must hit the  $2$ nd through  $\left(x-1\right)$ th RL diagonals,  $2$ nd through  $\left(y-x\right)$ th LR diagonals, and  $2$ nd through  $\left(y-1\right)$ th rows for a total of  $2y-5$  hits. This does not overcount because the line segment never hits any two rows or diagonals at the same time --- doing so would stop the line segment at that intersection, which never happens.

It is easy to see by induction that a coordinate  $\left(x,y\right)$  above corresponds to a reflected version of  $A$  precisely when  $x+y\equiv2\pmod3$ , a reflected version of  $B$  when  $x+y\equiv0\pmod3$ , and a reflected version of  $C$  when  $x+y\equiv1\pmod3$ . Furthermore, it is clear that  $\left(x,y\right)$  is the first time that the ray reaches a vertex if and only if there are no  $\left(x',y'\right)$  on the line between  $\left(1,1\right)$  and  $\left(x,y\right)$ . By taking an affine transformation, we can turn this into the Cartesian plane with these coordinates, so we need  $\gcd\left(x-1,y-1\right)=1$ . Thus, we want to find the different values of  $2y-5$  when  $x-1,y-1$  are relatively prime nonnegative integers,  $1\leq x\leq y$ , and  $x+y\equiv2\pmod3$ . Let  $a=x-1,b=y-1$ , so we want to find the different values of  $2b-3$  when  $a,b$  are relatively prime nonnegative integers with  $0\leq a\leq b$  and  $a+b\equiv0\pmod3$ .

If  $b\equiv0\pmod3$ , then  $a\equiv0\pmod3$ , so  $a,b$  are not relatively prime, contradiction.

If  $b\equiv2\pmod3$ , then take  $a=1$ . Then all conditions are satisfied, so this works. Thus, we can achieve all values of  $2b-3$  when  $b\equiv2\pmod3$ . This corresponds to all  $1\pmod6$  positive integers.

Now, assume that  $b\equiv1\pmod3$  and  $b\neq1,4,10$ .

Let  $p_1<p_2<p_3<\ldots$  be the  $2\pmod3$  primes. Let  $p_k$  be the smallest  $2\pmod3$  prime not dividing  $b$ , so  $p_1p_2\ldots p_{k-1}$  divides  $b$ .

If  $k=2$ , then  $b\equiv1\pmod3,b\equiv0\pmod2,b\not\equiv0\pmod5$ . Then  $b\equiv4\pmod6$ . Then  $b\geq16>5=p_2$ , so pick  $a=p_2$ .

The idea is to consider the reflection as actually reflecting the equilateral triangle across the side the path bounces off. Then, any such path is a straight line in the tesselation of the plane with these equilateral triangles. In other words, it suffices to find all  $n$  such that a straight segment in this tesselation between two image points of the starting vertex crosses exactly  $n$  lines, barring endpoints.

First, note that all images of the starting vertex form themselves an equilateral triangle tesselation of the plane. In particular, supposing that the equilateral triangle has side length 1, two of the vectors between two of these images are  $1+\omega$  and  $1-\omega^2 = 2-\omega$ , respectively, where  $\omega$  is a sixth root of unity. Therefore, the vector the path defines can be written as  $a(1+\omega) + b(2-\omega) = (a+2b)+(a-b)\omega$  for some nonnegative  $a, b$ .

Now, assume without loss of generality that  $a, b$  are positive and  $a \geq b$ . (If any  $n$  was reachable otherwise, we can reflect that path over a suitable line.) Then, notice that it crosses  $a+2b-1$  lines oriented in direction  $\omega$ ,  $a-b-1$  lines oriented in direction  $1$ , and  $3a+b-1$  lines oriented in direction  $\omega^2$ . As a result, the total number of lines is   $$ n = 2(2a+b) - 3. $$   Note that this obviously must be odd. On the other hand,  $2a+b \equiv b-a \pmod 3$ , and if  $a \equiv b \pmod 3$ , both  $a+2b$  and  $a-b$  are multiples of  $3$ , which implies that the path crosses some intermediate vertex, contradiction. This proves that  $n \equiv 1, 5\pmod 6$  is necessary.

We will show that the answer is all  $n \equiv 1 \pmod{6}$  and all  $n \equiv 5 \pmod{6}$  except for  $5,17.$ Construct a coordinate system with  $A=(0,0),B=(1,0),C=(1,1).$  Consider reflecting the triangle repeatedly, constructing a triangular lattice with  $A$  as its vertex and bounded by lines  $y=0$  and  $x=y.$  We can check that all points that are images of  $A$  satisfy  $x+y \equiv 0 \pmod{3}.$  Now, we may represent the reflections as drawing a segment between  $A$  and some image of  $A.$  We see that this path does not land on another vertex if the segment does not pass through a lattice point, which happens if and only if  $x,y$  are relatively prime. Now we may count the number of bounces as the number of intersections between a segment and a lattice line. A line from  $(0,0)$  to  $(a,b)$  intersects  $a-1$  lines of the form  $x=k, b-1$  lines of the form  $y=k$  and  $a-b-1$  lines of the form  $x-y=k,$  so it intersects  $2a-3$  lines total. Thus, our problem is reduced to finding all  $a$  such that there exists a  $k$  with  $a \ge k, \gcd{(a,k)}=1$  and  $a+k \equiv 0 \pmod{3},$  and for each  $a,$  we get a corresponding  $n=2a-3.$ First, if  $a \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$  then we must have  $k \equiv 0 \pmod{3},$  but that contradicts our relatively prime assumption, so there are no solutions in this case. If  $a \equiv 2 \pmod{3},$  we may choose  $k=1$  which always works. If  $a \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$  and  $a \ge 13,$  we may choose  $k=2$  when  $a \equiv 1 \pmod 6, k=\frac{n}{2}-3$  when  $a \equiv 4 \pmod{12},$  and  $k=\frac{n}{2}-6$  when  $a \equiv 10 \pmod{12}.$  We may manually check  $a=1,4,7,10$  and we find that  $a=1,4,10$  have no solutions and for  $a=7$  we can have  $k=2.$  Thus, we have  $a=1,2 \pmod{3}$  and  $a \ne 1,4,10.$  Finding our corresponding  $n$  for these values, we get  $n \equiv 1,5 \pmod{6}$  and  $n \ne 5,17.$
