The answer is all  $n$  divisible by  $3$ . For such  $n$ , just take the values  $a_i = 2$  if  $3 \mid i$  and  $a_i = -1$  if  $3 \nmid i$ .

Let  $n$  be not divisible by  $3$ . We consider the signs of the  $a_i$ 's and prove the following claims.

<u>Claim 1:</u> Among all  $a_i$ 's,  $0$  or  $1$  cannot occur.
WLOG say  $a_1 = 0$ . Then  $a_2 = a_3 = 1$  and all other  $a_i$ 's are positive. Thus  $a_{n-1}a_n + 1 > 0 = a_1$ . So  $0$  can't occur among the  $a_i$ 's. Then if  $1$  occurs for some  $a_i$ , then either  $a_{i-1}$  or  $a_{i-2}$  is  $0$  (with the indices in mod  $n$ ), contradicting the previous sentence.

<u>Claim 2:</u> No two consecutive  $a_i$ 's can be positive.
WLOG work with  $a_1$  and  $a_2$ . Both cannot be greater than  $1$  because the  $a_i$ 's will be increasing, contradicting  $a_{n-1}a_n + 1 = a_1$ . Both can't be less than  $1$  because then  $a_{n-1}, a_{n} > 1$ , which is bad from contradicting  $a_{n-1}a_n + 1 = a_1$ . Now suppose that  $a_1 < 1$  while  $a_2 > 1$ . Then  $a_{n-1}, a_n > 1$ , which is again bad. Now if  $a_1 > 1$  while  $a_2 < 1$ , we know that  $a_n > 1$ , contradicting  $a_na_1 + 1 = a_2$ . This claim is proved.

<u>Claim 3:</u> No three consecutive  $a_i$ 's can be negative.
WLOG work with  $a_1, a_2, a_3$ . From  $a_1a_2 + 1 = a_3$ , we have  $a_3$  positive, contradiction.

Thus, if we were to arrange the signs of  $a_1, ..., a_n$  in a circle clockwise, between every  $+$  must be at most two  $-$ . We then prove the next couple of claims, which are key to showing why  $n$  not divisible by  $3$  doesn't work. Consider the indices mod  $n$  from now on.

<u>Claim 4:</u> Any occurrence of a  $+-+$  and a  $--$  in the circle cannot happen.
So clearly, a  $--$  had to have been preceding a  $+-+$ . The  $a_i$  that corresponds to the last  $+$  must be less than  $1$  in magnitude since the previous two respective numbers  $a_{i-2}, a_{i-1}$  corresponding to the  $+-$  have a negative product, implying  $a_i = a_{i-2}a_{i-1} + 1 < 1$ . But then  $|a_{i-2}a_{i-1}| < 1$ . Since a  $--$  precedes  $a_{i-2}$ , we have  $|a_{i-2}| > 1$ . So then  $|a_{i-1}| < 1$ . The next member  $a_{i+1}$  must be negative from Claim 2, but this can't happen since  $|a_{i-1}| < 1$  and  $|a_{i}| < 1$ , contradiction. We've proved this claim.

<u>Claim 5:</u> We cannot alternate between  $+-+-...$  in the circle.
WLOG set  $a_i$  negative for  $i$  odd and  $a_i$  positive for  $i$  even. Then, for  $i$  odd, we need  $|a_ia_{i+1}| > 1$  and for  $i$  even, we need  $|a_ia_{i+1}| < 1$ . For  $i$  even,  $|a_i| < 1$  so then for  $i$  odd,  $|a_i| > 1$ . But then, for this to hold,  $|a_ia_{i+1}| > 2$  for  $i$  odd. For this to hold,  $|a_i| > 2$  needs to be true for  $i$  odd. Repeat this logic, and we have that  $|a_i|$  must be infinitely large for  $i$  odd, which is bad. This last claim is proven.

From Claims 4 and 5, the only valid arrangement of  $+$  and  $-$  is  $+--+--...$  which happens only if  $3 \mid n$ . We are done.

The answer is all multiples of three; an example is  $-1, -1, 2, \dots$ .

Suppose  $3 \nmid n$ . Note that
\begin{align*}
	a_k a_{k+1} a_{k+2} + a_{k+2} & = a_{k+2}^2
	a_k a_{k+1} a_{k+2} + a_k & = a_k a_{k+3}
\end{align*}
by the given for  $k$  and  $k+1$ .

Summing both statements over all  $k$ ,
\[\sum_k a_k^2 = \sum_k a_k a_{k+3} \implies \sum_k (a_k - a_{k+3})^2 = 0\]
and so  $a_k = a_{k+3}$  for all  $k$ .

If  $3 \nmid n$  it follows that sequence must be a constant  $x$ , but then  $x^2 + 1 \neq x$ . Hence  $3 \nmid n$  is not possible.

Well many people probably have solutions on sign treatment but let me post mine too, for completeness. The construction when  $3|n$  is simply  $(2, -1, -1)$ , repeat. For the rest of the proof, we visualize the numbers  $a_1, a_2, \cdots , a_n$  on a circle (which means we can repeat the cycle as many times as we want), and show that the signs must be in the cycle of  $--+$ . 

We first eliminate the case where  $a_i=0$  for some  $i$ . W.L.O.G. let  $a_1=0$ . Then we must have  $a_2=a_3=1$  and  $a_4=2$ , etc. Now some inductive statement shows that if  $a_i, a_{i+1}>0$  then  $a_{i+2}>0$ , and we also have  $a_2>0$  too. Hence  $a_i>0$  for all  $i>0$ , including when  $i=n+1$ , contradiction. 

Now we eliminate the case where  $a_i, a_{i+1}>0$  for some  $i$ . Again here we consider indices mod  $n$ . Now  $a_{i+2}>1$ , and therefore  $a_{i+3}>1$ . Subsequently, we have  $a_{i+4}=a{i+2}a{i+3}+1>a{i+2}a{i+3}\ge a{i+3}\ge 1$ , which shows that this sequence is actually increasing after  $a_{i+3}$ . This cannot happen since the sequence of real numbers are on a circle. 

This therefore imply that between any two positive numbers there must be at least one negative number; if  $a_{i}, a_{i+1}<0$  then  $a_{i+2}=a_{i}a_{i+1}+1>1$ , so there must be at most two negative numbers between any two consecutive positive numbers. As the goal is to show that there are exactly two negative numbers between any two consecutive positive numbers, it suffices to show that the configuration  $+-+$  cannot happen. To do this we do 'backtracking', i.e. consider  $a_i, a_{i-1}, a_{i-2}$ , etc, given the circular structure of our sequence. 

Now suppose that  $a_{i+2}>0$  and  $a_{i+1}<0$  and  $a_i>0$ . We first see that  $a_ia_{i+1}<0$  so  $a_{i+2}<1$ . Also  $a_{i+3}<0$  by the ''no consecutive positive'' lemma we established in the beginning. This means,  $a_{i+1}a_{i+2}<-1$  and with  $a_{i+2}<1$  (comparing modulus) we get  $a_{i+1}<-1$ , actually. Now that  $a_i=\frac{a_{i+2}-1}{a_{i+1}}$  with  $|a_{i+2}-1|<1$  (since  $0<a_{i+2}<1$ ) and  $|a_{i+1}|>1$  as proven we have  $|a_i|<1$ ; combining this with  $a_i>0$  we get  $0<a_i<1$ . Going a bit further,  $a_{i-1}=\frac{a_{i+1}-1}{a_{i}}$ ;  $a_{i+1}<0$  so  $|a_{i+1}-1|=|a_{i+1}|+1$ ; and  $0<a_i<1$  so  $|a_{i-1}|=\frac{|a_{i+1}-1|}{|a_{i}|}>|a_{i+1}|+1$ , and bear in mind that  $a_{i-1}<0$  here. Therefore  $a_{i-1} <a_{i+1}-1$ , i.e. getting more negative. Continuing this backtracking process, we see that the numbers must be alternating in sign, with positive numbers bounded above by 1, and negative numbers given by  $a_{i-1} <a_{i+1}-1$  whenever both numbers are negative. This cannot happen on a circle, reaching our contradiction. 

Hence the sign must be a cycle of length 3, proving that  $3|n$ .

Suppose  $a_{2\ell}\geqslant 0$  and  $a_{2\ell+1}<0$  for all  $\ell$ .
Then,  $a_{2k} = a_{2k-1}a_{2k-2}+1 \leqslant 1$  for all  $k\geqslant 1$ , so  $a_{2k+1} = a_{2k}a_{2k-1} + 1 \geqslant a_{2k-1} + 1$  for all  $k\geqslant 1$ .
This forces  $0 > a_{2k+1} \geqslant a_1 + k$  for all  $k$ , which is clearly impossible.

Therefore the sequence of signs has to be  $+,-,-,+,-,-,\cdots$ , hence  $n$  is divisible by  $3$ , which is possible from the example  $2,-1,-1,2,-1,-1,\cdots$ .  $\blacksquare$

Note that the recursion implies  $a_ia_{i+1}a_{i+2}+a_{i+2}=a_{i+2}^2$  and  $a_{i-1}a_ia_{i+1}+a_{i-1}=a_{i-1}a_{i+2}$ . Summing both of these up over all indices  $i$ , the LHS are equivalent, so we get   $$ \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2=\sum_{i=1}^n a_ia_{i+3} $$  This is equivalent to  $\sum_{i=1}^n (a_i-a_{i+3})^2=0$ , so if  $3\not\arrowvert n$ , we must have  $a_1=a_2=\ldots=a_n=k$ , and otherwise we have  $a_1=a_4=\ldots; a_2=a_5=\ldots; a_3=a_6=\ldots$ . The former is impossible, as  $k^2+1=k$  yields imaginary  $k$ . For the latter, we get the construction  $(2,-1,-1,\ldots, 2, -1, -1)$ . So, our answer is all multiples of 3.

Anyway, here's my solution: We'll extend the indices to all integers, and work on an index modulo  $n$  while applying the recursion given. The answer is all  $n$  divisible by  $3$ . The construction for  $n=3m$  is  $a_{3k}=2$  for all  $k \in [m]$ , and  $-1$  otherwise, which clearly works. Now, we show that no other  $n$  works. We will move through a series of claims to do so.**CLAIM 1** We cannot have both  $a_i,a_{i+1}$  as non-negative numbers (where  $i \in \mathbb{Z}$ ).

<u>Proof of Claim 1-</u> FTSOC assume that  $a_1,a_2 \geq 0$  (taking  $i=1$  WLOG). Then, from our recursion, all  $a_i$ 's for  $i \geq 3$  must be positive, and atleast equal to  $1$ . But then  $a_{i+2}=a_{i+1}a_i+1 \geq a_{i+1}+1$  for  $i \geq 3$  which means that the sequence is strictly increasing for sufficiently large  $i$ . However, this will eventually give us  $a_1>a_1$ , a contradiction.**CLAIM 2** We cannot have  $a_i=0$  for any  $i \in \mathbb{Z}$ .

<u>Proof of Claim 2-</u> FTSOC assume we have  $a_i=0$ . Then  $a_{i+1}=a_{i-1}a_i+1=1$ , which means that both  $a_i,a_{i+1}$  are non-negative numbers, contrary to Claim 1.

From now on, we'll assume that none of the  $a_i$ 's are zero (as per Claim 2).**CLAIM 3** We cannot have  $a_i>0,a_{i+1}<0$  and  $a_{i+2}>0$  for any  $i \in \mathbb{Z}$ .

<u>Proof of Claim 3-</u> FTSOC assume that such an index  $i$  exists. Let  $b_k=|a_k|$  for all  $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ . Note that, by Claim 1, we must have  $a_{i-1}<0$  and  $a_{i+3}<0$ . Then the problem condition translates to   $$ b_ib_{i+1}+b_{i+2}=1 \text{ and } b_{i+1}b_{i+2}=1+b_{i+3} $$  Subtracting the first equation from the second equation, we get   $$ b_{i+2}-b_i=\frac{b_{i+2}+b_{i+3}}{b_{i+1}}>0 \Rightarrow b_{i+2}>b_i $$  Thus, we have   $$ 1=b_ib_{i+1}+b_{i+2}>b_i(b_{i+1}+1)>b_i $$  Also,  $b_i+a_{i-2}b_{i-1}=1$ . Since  $0<b_i<1$  and  $b_{i-1}>0$ , so we must have  $a_{i-2}>0$ . Thus, we get the triple  $\{a_{i-2},a_{i-1},a_i\}$  with signs  $a_{i-2}>0,a_{i-1}<0$  and  $a_i>0$ . Then we can continue in this manner to get  $a_j>0$  iff  $2 \mid i-j$ . This means that we get a sequence with alternating  $+$  and  $-$  signs. Note that for this to happen  $n$  must be even (else we get  $a_1>0>a_n+1$ , which is not possible). WLOG assume  $a_1<0$ . Then we have  $a_{2k}>0$  and  $a_{2k-1}<0$  for all  $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ . 

Now,  $b_1b_2=1+b_3$ , which gives  $b_1b_2>1$ . Similarly, we can show  $b_3b_4,b_5b_6, \dots ,b_{n-1}b_n>1$ . Since all  $b_k$ 's are positive, so multiplying these inequalities gives  $b_1b_2 \dots b_n>1$ . Again, we have  $b_2b_3+b_4=1$ , which means  $b_2b_3<1$ . In a similar fashion, we get  $b_4b_5, \dots ,b_nb_1<1$ . And, multiplying these inequalities gives  $b_1b_2 \dots b_n<1$ . Thus, we arrive at a contradiction, as desired.**CLAIM 4** Note that all  $a_i$ 's cannot be negative (Since if  $a_1,a_2<0$ , then  $a_3>0$ ). WLOG take  $a_1>0$ . Then  $a_{3k+1}>0$  for  $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ , and all other  $a_i$ 's are negative.

<u>Proof of Claim 4-</u> By Claim 1, we must have  $a_2<0$ . Then Claim 3 gives  $a_3<0$ , while using  $a_4=a_2a_3+1$ , we get  $a_4>0$ . Continuing in this fashion, we get the desired claim.

Now, we are almost done. Suppose some  $n$  works, and WLOG take  $a_1>0$ . Then  $a_{n+1}>0$  gives  $3 \mid (n+1)-1=n$  (Using Claim 4). Hence, done.  $\blacksquare$

Therefore we can have the sign configuration  $-,-,+$  that is periodic  $\pmod{3}$ .
- If  $a_1>0,a_2<0$  or  $+,-,\dots$ . If the sequence sign is alternating,  we have  $a_3=a_1a_2+1>0$ , thus  $a_1a_2>-1$ . Then we have  $a_4=a_2a_3+1<0$ , so  $a_2a_3<-1<a_1a_2$ . solution_md: The answer is no. Let $N = 1 + 2 + \dots + 2018$ . Call a number *good* if it is one of $1$ , $2$ , $\dots$ , $2018$ and *suspicious* if it is one of $N$ , $N - 1$ , $\dots$ , $N - 2018$ . Draw an arrow from each number not in the bottom row to the greater of the two numbers below that number, which we will term its *support*. Observe that the absolute difference of any two suspicious numbers is a good number and that the support of a suspicious number is always a suspicious number.**Claim:** There is exactly one good number in each row. *Proof.* Consider the chain starting with the topmost number. Let $a_1$ , $a_2$ , $\dots$ , $a_{2018}$ be the numbers in this chain, from top to bottom. Note that \begin{align*}a_{2018} = (a_{2018} - a_{2017}) + (a_{2017} - a_{2016}) + \dots + (a_2 - a_1) + a_1 \geq 1 + 2 + \dots + 2018\end{align*} since $a_{2018} - a_{2017}$ , $a_{2017} - a_{2016}$ , $\dots$ , $a_2 - a_1$ and $a_1$ are all numbers in the array in different rows. As equality must hold, this proves the claim. $\square$ **Claim:** There are at most $1010$ suspicious numbers in the bottom row. *Proof.* This is a trivial consequence of the fact that there is at most one pair of adjacent suspicious numbers, which is because otherwise there would be two good numbers in the row above. $\square$ **Claim:** Every suspicious number is in one of the bottom $64$ rows. *Proof.* Consider a suspicious number and the chain starting therewith. Let $a_1$ , $a_2$ , $\dots$ , $a_k$ be the numbers in this chain, from top to bottom. Note that \begin{align*}a_k = (a_k - a_{k - 1}) + (a_{k - 1} - a_{k - 2}) + \dots + (a_2 - a_1) + a_1 \geq 1 + 2 + \dots + (k - 1) + a_1\end{align*} since $a_k - a_{k - 1}$ , $a_{k - 1} - a_{k - 2}$ , $\dots$ , $a_2 - a_1$ and $a_1$ are all numbers in the array in different rows. This implies that $2018 \geq N - a_1 \geq 1 + 2 + \dots + (k - 1)$ , whence $k \leq 64$ , as desired. $\square$ **Claim:** In each of these $64$ rows but the bottommost, there are at most two suspicious numbers. *Proof.* Suppose that in some row, there are three suspicious numbers, $a$ , $b$ and $c$ , and let their supports be $a'$ , $b'$ and $c'$ , respectively. Clearly, $a'$ , $b'$ and $c'$ are also suspicious. Now, consider the number $A$ that the arrow $a \to a'$ flanks. Obviously, it is one of $a' \pm a$ , so for $a' + a > N$ , it has to be $a' - a$ . Similarly, note that the arrows $b \to b'$ and $c \to c'$ flank $B = b' - b$ and $C = c' - c$ , respectively. If $A = B = C$ , then this number would be flanked on three sides with arrows, which cannot happen. However, $A$ , $B$ and $C$ are all good, so some row has at least two good numbers, contradiction. $\square$ Therefore, there are at most $1010 + 2 \cdot (64 - 1) = 1136$ suspicious numbers. Contradiction.

Assume such a thing exists.  Start at the top, at a point  $x=a_1$ .  Now, for  $1 \le k \le 2017$  if we are on a point  $a_1+ \cdots +a_k$  in the  $k$ th row, then let  $a_{k+1}$  be the smaller of the two entries below us and move to  $a_1+ \cdots +a_{k+1}$ .  We end up at  $a_1 + \cdots +a_{2018} \ge 1+2+ \cdots +2018$ , so it follows that the  $a_i$  are a permutation of  $[2018]$ .  Call this the  $\emph{middle sequence}$ .

Now, consider the leftmost element of the  $1010$ th row,  $L$ .  Starting at  $L$ , create the  $\emph{left sequence}$  as follows.  Repeatedly go down from an element to the larger child, and note that since we go down  $1008$  times we either increment by at least  $2009+ \cdots +3016$  which is too much, so at some point we run into the middle sequence. Similarly if we let  $R$  be the rightmost element of the  $1010$ th row and construct a right sequence, this also will intersect the middle sequence.  Now, let  $L_1$  and  $R_1$  be the equilateral triangles along the base and sides with  $L,R$  as their top vertices.  Then the left and right sequences are contained in these triangles, and so the middle sequence must intersect both triangles.  But this is easily seen to be a contradiction, as once any of these sequences hits one of these triangles it stays there.  We are done.

Consider any anti-Pascal triangle with  $n$  rows.
Let  $a_k$  and  $b_k$  denote the maximum and minimum number in row  $k$ .
Clearly,  $a_{k-1} \leqslant a_k-b_k$  for all  $k$ , so  $a_k \geqslant a_{k-1}+b_k$  for all  $k$ .
Summing this for  $k=2,\ldots,n$  and noting that  $a_1=b_1$ , we have  $$ a_n \geqslant b_1 + b_2 +\cdots + b_n. $$  Now, suppose there exist an anti-Pascal triangle with  $2018$  rows containing every integer from  $1$  to  $1+2+\cdots +2018$ .
Define  $a_k,b_k$  as above; we will have  $$ a_{2018} \geqslant b_1 + b_2 +\cdots + b_{2018}\geqslant 1+2+\cdots +2018. $$  However,  $1+2+\cdots+2018$  is precisely the maximum possible value of  $a_{2018}$ , so all the inequalities above are equalities, and so for each  $k\geqslant 2$ ,
(i)  $a_k$  and  $b_k$  are consecutive elements of the triangle, and
(ii)  $a_{k-1}$  lie directly above  $a_k$  and  $b_k$ .
Hence all numbers  $a_k$  and  $b_k$  are in a "strand" of width from top to bottom of the triangle. 
In particular, it is possible to find a sub-triangle with  $1008=\left\lceil\frac{2018-2}{2}\right\rceil$  rows not containing any of  $\{1,2,\ldots,2018\}$ .

Re-defining  $a_k$  and  $b_k$  again for this sub-triangle, we have  $$ a_{1008} \geqslant b_1 + b_2 +\cdots + b_{1008} \geqslant 2019 + 2020 +\cdots +3026 > \frac{2018\cdot 2019}{2} $$  which is clearly impossible. Therefore there are no anti-Pascal triangles with  $2018$  rows containing every integer from  $1$  to  $1 + 2 + 3 + \dots + 2018.$   $\blacksquare$

There does not exists such an anti-Pascal triangle.

First of all we will study some properties of anti-Pascal triangles. Consider an  $n$ -rows ant-Pascal triangle with different numbers as entries and define a sequence  $b_n$  and  $s_n$  as follows.

Let  $b_1 = s_1$  be the number at apex. Considering two numbers at left below and right below of  $b_1$ , let  $b_2$  be the bigger one and  $s_1$  be the smaller one. And then, considering two numbers at left below and right below of  $b_2$ , let  $b_3$  be the bigger one and  $s_3$  be the smaller one. Likewise, for each  $k=1,2, \ldots, n-1$  considering two numbers in the  $k+1$ th row which are below  $b_k$ , let  $b_{k+1}$  be the bigger one and  $s_{k+1}$  be the smaller one. Then we can observe the following; if the followings are the smallest numbers in the anti-Pascal triangle
\[
       m_1 < m_2 < \ldots <m_n,
\]
then
\[ b_n = b_{n-1}+s_n = b_{n-2}+s_{n-1}+s_n= \cdots = s_1+s_2+\cdots +s_n \ge m_1+m_2+ \cdots +m_n \]
We call the sequence  $b_1, b_2, \ldots , b_n$ , the  $b$  sequence of the triangle and call  $s_1$ ,  $s_2$ ,  $\ldots$ ,  $s_n$  be the  $s$  sequence of the triangle. We also call the number  $b_n$  the big of the triangle.

Now let  $n = 2018$  and assume that there is an anti-Pascal triangle which are described in the problem, say  $\Delta$ . Let the  $b$  sequence of  $\Delta$  be  $b_1 , b_2 , \ldots , b_n$  and  $s$ -sequence of  $\Delta$  be  $s_1, s_2 , \ldots , s_n$ . Then because,
\[\frac{n(n+1)}{2} \ge b_n = s_1 +s_2 + \cdots + s_n \ge 1+2+ \cdots + n \]
and the equality holds, we have
\[ \left\{s_1 , s_2, \ldots , s_n\right\} = \left\{1,2, \ldots , n\right\} \]
We call the positions occupied by  $s$  sequence and  $b$  sequence the main stream. In the  $n$ th row, there are  $n-2$  numbers except for  $s_n$  and  $b_n$ . Then there exists at least one and at most two anti-Pascal triangles constructed from those  $n-2$  numbers to upward. Let those anti-Pascal triangles be  $L$  and  $R$ . Let the big of  $L$  and  $R$  be  $b^L$  and  $b^R$  and let  $M=b^L + b^R$ . Since the sum of the number of rows of  $L$  and  $R$  is  $n-2$  and they does not meet the main stream of  $\Delta$ , we have
        \[ M \ge (n+1)+(n+2) + \cdots + (2n-2) = \frac{1}{2} (n-2) (3 n-1) \]
However, the maximum entry of  $\Delta$  is  $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$  and it is already positioned on the main stream, so
        \[ M \le \frac{n(n+1)}{2}-1 + \frac{n(n+1)}{2}-2\]
i.e.
        \[ \frac{n(n+1)}{2} -1 + \frac{n(n+1)}{2}-2 \le \frac{1}{2} (n-2) (3 n-1) \]
It follows that  $n \le 8$  which is an absurdity.
This completes the proof.

Define a special anti-pascal triangle of size  $n$  as an anti-pascal triangle with  $n$  rows and having each number from  $1$  to  $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$  numbers exactly once. Now, consider a special anti-pascal triangle of size  $n$ . For each number in the anti-pascal triangle, it will have two numbers beneath it (on the right and the left), unless it's on the bottom row. Now, draw an arrow between each number and the larger of the two numbers below it. Finally, place a  $0$  on row  $0$  (above the first row), and connect an arrow from it to the first number.

Define the weight of an edge as the difference between the bottom number and the top. Then, this is equal to the third number (the smaller of the two bottom numbers). Consider the path from  $0$  to the bottom of the anti-pascal triangle. Since each number on this anti-pascal  is distinct, the path will contain distinct elements. Furthermore, since it starts at  $0$ , and contains  $n$  edges, the minimum sum of weights will be  $1 + 2 + \ldots n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ . Since the largest number is  $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$  anyway, the number of edge weights is a permutation of  $\{1,2,\ldots n\}$ . 

Now, since this edge weights are from  $1$  to  $n$ , this also means each row contains exactly one element of  $\{1,2,\ldots n\}$ . A corrolarly of this is that the smallest element in each row is between  $1$  and  $n$ .

We can now show by induction that the largest and smallest numbers of each row are adjacent, and the largest one is on the path starting at  $0$ . Our base case is the nth row: our path starting at  $0$  ends at  $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ , which is the largest element, and furthermore since the number from  $\{1,2,\ldots n\}$  in the nth row must be the smallest, and will be also adjacent to  $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$  (by definition of edge weight), this proves the base case. For our inductive step, we assume on row  $i$  the smallest element is adjacent to the largest, which is on the path. Now, clearly by subtracting these two, we will get the largest absolute difference on row  $i-1$ . Furthermore, again due to the edge weight definitions, it must be adjacent to a number next to  $\{1,2,\ldots n\}$ , which is the smallest in that row. This completes the induction.

WLOG, let the path starting at  $0$  end on the right part of the last row (so it will be to the right of the axis of symmetry). We assume  $n$  is even (since  $n = 2018$  is even), which means it can not be on the exact middle of the last row. Consider taking a path that goes through the first (and hence the leftmost) element of the  $\frac{n}{2} + 2$ th row. Clearly, this path can not join with the path starting from  $0$  (since we assume it ended on the right section of the last row), so each edge weight must be at least  $(n+1)$ . However, there are  $\frac{n}{2} - 2$  edges in this path, so if  $A$  was the last number on this path, we have the following inequality:
\[A\geq (n+1) + (n+2) + \ldots + (n + \frac{n}{2} - 1) = \frac{n^2 - n}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{n}{2}\cdot \frac{n-2}{2} = \frac{5n^2 - 7n}{8}\]
Finally, observe that for  $n = 2018$ , we have  $\frac{5n^2 - 7n}{8} > \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ , which means  $A$  can not be in this anti-pascal triangle, a contradiction. Therefore, we conclude no such anti-pascal triangle exist.

<details><summary>solution</summary>Standard asymptotic notation ( $O, \Omega, \Theta$ ) throughout.

We'll show that for sufficiently large  $n$ , there is no anti-Pascal triangle with  $n$  rows. Suppose otherwise, and that there is such an anti-Pascal triangle. Let  $m=n(n+1)/2$  be the number of entries in the triangle. Call a number in the triangle *big* if it is greater than  $m/2$  and *small* otherwise (so, about half the numbers are big and half are small). Note that each big number which is not in the bottom row must be above one small number and one big number. Now, the intuition of the proof proceeds as follows: if a number is very big (close to  $m$ ), then it must be the difference between an even bigger number and an even smaller number. We will show that there is not enough "bigness" and "smallness" to generate all these big numbers as differences.

More concretely, say that every big number *covers* the two numbers below it. Then, if a big number  $k$  covers a big number  $i$  and a small number  $j$ , we have  $m-k = (m-i) + j$ . Here  $m-k$  and  $m-i$  measure the "bignesses" of  $k$  and  $i$ . Also, let  $r$  be the number of big numbers in the bottom row (so  $r \le n$ ), and let  $s = \lfloor m/2 \rfloor - r = n^2/4 - O(n)$  be the number of big numbers which are not in the bottom row. So, these  $s$  big numbers cover one big and one small number each.

Now, we sum the identity  $m-k = (m-i) + j$  over all  $k$  which cover big  $i$  and small  $j$ . We have:
\[\sum_{\text{big  $k$  not in bottom row}} (m-k) = \sum_{\text{ $k$  covers big  $i$ }} (m-i) + \sum_{\text{ $k$  covers small  $j$ }} j.\]
Let  $A$  and  $B$  be the values of the two sums on the RHS above, respectively. Then  $A$  is the sum of  $m-i$  over all covered big  $i$ , with multiplicity, and  $B$  is the sum of all covered small numbers with multiplicity. Since there are  $s$  covered big and small numbers, and each number is covered at most twice, we can get lower bounds on  $A$  and  $B$ :
\[A \ge 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 2 + \dots + (\lfloor s/2 \rfloor - 1) = n^4/16 + O(n^3),\]
\[B \ge 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + \dots + \lfloor s/2 \rfloor = n^4/16 + O(n^3).\]
On the other hand  $A+B$  is the RHS of the earlier equation, so
\[A+B \le \sum_{\text{big  $k$ }} (m-k) = 0 + 1 + 2 + \dots + (\lceil m/2 \rceil - 1) = n^4/8 + O(n^3).\]
Note that the upper bound and lower bound for  $A+B$  are very close together: they are only  $O(n^3)$  apart, while the quantity is  $\Theta(n^4)$ . So for the triangle to exist, the lower bounds on  $A$  and  $B$  have to be pretty tight. Now, for the remainder of the proof, we'll try to fudge the lower bounds on  $A$  and  $B$  up by a little to obtain a contradiction.

Define a *type 1* number to be a small number above  $s/2+n^{3/2}$  or a big number below  $m - s/2 - n^{3/2}$  which is covered. solutionStandard asymptotic notation ( $O, \Omega, \Theta$ ) throughout. We'll show that for sufficiently large $n$ , there is no anti-Pascal triangle with $n$ rows. Suppose otherwise, and that there is such an anti-Pascal triangle. Let $m=n(n+1)/2$ be the number of entries in the triangle. Call a number in the triangle *big* if it is greater than $m/2$ and *small* otherwise (so, about half the numbers are big and half are small). Note that each big number which is not in the bottom row must be above one small number and one big number. Now, the intuition of the proof proceeds as follows: if a number is very big (close to $m$ ), then it must be the difference between an even bigger number and an even smaller number. We will show that there is not enough "bigness" and "smallness" to generate all these big numbers as differences. More concretely, say that every big number *covers* the two numbers below it. Then, if a big number $k$ covers a big number $i$ and a small number $j$ , we have $m-k = (m-i) + j$ . Here $m-k$ and $m-i$ measure the "bignesses" of $k$ and $i$ . Also, let $r$ be the number of big numbers in the bottom row (so $r \le n$ ), and let $s = \lfloor m/2 \rfloor - r = n^2/4 - O(n)$ be the number of big numbers which are not in the bottom row. So, these $s$ big numbers cover one big and one small number each. Now, we sum the identity $m-k = (m-i) + j$ over all $k$ which cover big $i$ and small $j$ . We have: \[\sum_{\text{big $k$ not in bottom row}} (m-k) = \sum_{\text{ $k$ covers big $i$ }} (m-i) + \sum_{\text{ $k$ covers small $j$ }} j.\] Let $A$ and $B$ be the values of the two sums on the RHS above, respectively. Then $A$ is the sum of $m-i$ over all covered big $i$ , with multiplicity, and $B$ is the sum of all covered small numbers with multiplicity. Since there are $s$ covered big and small numbers, and each number is covered at most twice, we can get lower bounds on $A$ and $B$ : \[A \ge 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 2 + \dots + (\lfloor s/2 \rfloor - 1) = n^4/16 + O(n^3),\] \[B \ge 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + \dots + \lfloor s/2 \rfloor = n^4/16 + O(n^3).\] On the other hand $A+B$ is the RHS of the earlier equation, so \[A+B \le \sum_{\text{big $k$ }} (m-k) = 0 + 1 + 2 + \dots + (\lceil m/2 \rceil - 1) = n^4/8 + O(n^3).\] Note that the upper bound and lower bound for $A+B$ are very close together: they are only $O(n^3)$ apart, while the quantity is $\Theta(n^4)$ . So for the triangle to exist, the lower bounds on $A$ and $B$ have to be pretty tight. Now, for the remainder of the proof, we'll try to fudge the lower bounds on $A$ and $B$ up by a little to obtain a contradiction. Define a *type 1* number to be a small number above $s/2+n^{3/2}$ or a big number below $m - s/2 - n^{3/2}$ which is covered. Let a *type 2* number be a small number below $s/2 - n^{3/2}$ or a big number above $m - s/2 + n^{3/2}$ which is not covered twice (i.e., is covered by zero or one big numbers). There may be at most $O(n^{3/2})$ type 1 and type 2 numbers, since otherwise we can increase the lower bound on $A$ or $B$ by $\Omega(n^3)$ and contradict the upper bound on $A+B$ . Since there are $O(n^{3/2})$ type 2 numbers, there must be at least $s/2 - O(n^{3/2}) = \Omega(n^2)$ small numbers $a$ which are covered twice. Moreover, at most $O(n^{3/2})$ of these choices for $a$ are covered by some number which is in the range $[m/2 + s/2 - n^{3/2}, m - s/2 + n^{3/2}]$ (since this range has size $O(n^{3/2})$ ). Thus, there are at least $\Omega(n^2)$ small $a$ which are covered by two numbers which are each in either $(m/2, m/2 + s/2 - n^{3/2})$ or $(m-s/2+n^{3/2}, m]$ . Now, consider the five numbers above such a choice for $a$ ( $d$ and $f$ may not exist): ``` d e f b c a ``` Since $b, c$ are big (since they cover $a$ ), $e$ must be small. If either $b$ or $c$ is in the range $(m-s/2+n^{3/2}, m]$ , then it is a type 2 number, since $e$ is small and thus does not cover it. Otherwise, $b$ and $c$ are both in $(m/2, m/2 + s/2 - n^{3/2})$ , in which case we must have $e < s/2 - n^{3/2}$ . Then, either $e$ is type 2, or it is covered twice, in which case $d$ and $f$ must both exist and be big. But then $b$ (and also $c$ ) is covered, so it is type 1. Thus, for each of the $\Omega(n^2)$ choices for $a$ , we can find a corresponding type 1 or 2 number, which is either $b$ , $c$ , or $e$ . Obviously each type 1 or 2 number corresponds to at most 3 choices for $a$ , but in order for $n=2018$ to be big enough for the argument to work, we need to make a slightly stronger statement. Indeed, note that each big type 1 or 2 number obtained this way (which must be $b$ or $c$ ) must correspond to the small number which it covers. We call a number *tiny* if it is  $\leq 2018$  and *massive* if it is  $\geq 1009\cdot 2019-2018$ .**Claim:  $\min(i)$  is tiny for  $i=1,2,\dots,2018$ .**
Proof: Note that   $$ \max(i) \leq \max(i+1) -\min(i+1) $$    $$  \max(i+1)\geq \max(i) + \min(i+1) $$     $$ 1+2+3+\dots+2018 \geq \max(2018) \geq \sum \min(i) \geq 1+2+3+\dots+2018 $$  which implies that equality must hold and as such our claim must be true.**Claim: There are at most  $2$  massive numbers in every row except possibly the bottom row.**

Proof: Note that two adjacent massive numbers forms a tiny number on top of the two massive numbers. 

However, note that the second last row only has one tiny number. Therefore, there can be only  $1$  pair of adjacent massive numbers.

Hence, we have at most   $\frac{2018}{2}+1=1010$  massive numbers in the bottom row.**Claim: If  $x\geq i+(i+1)+...2018$ ,  $x$  must be at most  $i$  rows from the bottom row**

Then
\begin{align*}
x_k &= x+(x_2-x_1)+(x_3-x_2)+\dots+(xk-x{k-1}) 
&\geq \big(i+(i+1)+\dots+2018\big)+\big(1+2+3+\dots +(k-1)\big)

a contradiction.

The answer is definitely not. Fix  $n = 2018$ .

Consider a path starting from the topmost value, going downwards towards the larger value. As we move down this path, color the numbers we cross green. For each green number, color the other cell directly beneath it purple. We call this the **grapevine.** $\textbf{Claim.}$  The integers  $1$  through  $n$  appear exactly once in the grapevine. $\textit{Proof.}$  We add the purple numbers to the number up top to get the number at the bottom of the grapevine. This sum is at least  $1 + 2 + \dots + n$ , but this is the maximum value of the triangle. It follows that equality must hold, i.e. the grapes must consist of a permutation of  $1$  through  $n$  (including the top number.)

Now consider the bottom row, split into three pieces: pre-grapevine, grapevine, post-grapevine. One of these three pieces has length at least  $1008$ , so there exists a subtriangle of size  $1008$ . We consider a grapevine in this subtriangle. The sum of the grapes, including the top number, is at least
\[ 2019 + 2020 + \dots + (2018 + 1008) = 2018 \cdot 1008 + \frac{1008 \cdot 1009}{2} = 1009(2016 + 504) = 1009(2520) > \frac{2018 \cdot 2019}{2}. \] This is too big. Thus unfortunately we can make no wine, as desired.

stem_md:
A *site* is any point  $(x, y)$  in the plane such that  $x$  and  $y$  are both positive integers less than or equal to 20.

Initially, each of the 400 sites is unoccupied. Amy and Ben take turns placing stones with Amy going first. On her turn, Amy places a new red stone on an unoccupied site such that the distance between any two sites occupied by red stones is not equal to  $\sqrt{5}$ . On his turn, Ben places a new blue stone on any unoccupied site. (A site occupied by a blue stone is allowed to be at any distance from any other occupied site.) They stop as soon as a player cannot place a stone.

Find the greatest  $K$  such that Amy can ensure that she places at least  $K$  red stones, no matter how Ben places his blue stones.

*Proposed by Gurgen Asatryan, Armenia*
solution_md:
I claim that our answer is  $\boxed{K = 100}$ . This can clearly be done by coloring every other square in every other row red. Now we show that  $100$  is indeed the maximum.

Consider a  $4$  by  $4$  grid, say the set of lattice points  $1 \leq x, y \leq 4$ . Consider squares\[(2, 1) \to (4, 2) \to (3, 4) \to (1, 3)\]\[(1,2) \to (3,1) \to (4,3) \to (2,4)\]and rhombi\[(1, 1) \to (3, 2) \to (4,4) \to (2,3)\]\[(4, 1) \to (3,3) \to (1,4) \to (2,2).\]Let the vertices of these four shapes form four sets of points (4 points each), labeled  $S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4$ , respectively. Note that when Amy picks a point in set  $S_i$  then Ben can just pick the point in that set farthest away from Amy's point. Then, Amy can pick at most one point from each set, hence at most  $4$  points in any  $4$  by  $4$  if Ben plays wisely. 

Since the original  $20$  by  $20$  site can be split into  $25$  grids of size  $4$  by  $4$ , given that Ben plays wisely, the maximum number of red points Amy can pick is indeed  $25 \cdot 4 = 100$  as desired.  $\blacksquare$

The problem is about chessboard and placing knights that don't hit each other :D
My solution is based on this observation. I remember that some years ago I saw the following problem: "How many knights can be placed on a chess board such that they don't attack each other?" The answer was $32$ for a $8 \times 8$ table. For a $20 \times 20$ table the answer should be $200$ and here is the proof: If we look at a $2 \times 4$ block, it's easy to conclude that we can place at most $4$ knights such that they don't attack each other. So if we divide out board into $50$ such blocks, we conclude that on a $20 \times 20$ board we can place at most $200$ knights such that they don't attack each other. And of course, such a configuration is possible: If the table is black and white (like a chess board), we can place all the knights on the same color. Let's say that $A$ is the set of all configurations in which there are placed $200$ knights on the board such that they don't attack each other. (I guess that $A$ has only two elements, but this is not relevant. What is relevant is that $A$ is not empty.) Now, in the hypothetical case in which Amy plays alone (i.e. Ben doesn't place any stone on the board), Amy could place at most $200$ stones. Coming back to the original problem (in which Amy plays along with Ben): Amy has to choose a configuration from $A$ and to follow it in order to maximize the " $K$ ". In order to minimize her " $K$ ", Ben has to place stones on the same configuration as Amy. However, at every turn, Ben can only decrease $K$ with $1.$ So $K \le 100.$ $K=100$ is possible: She just has to place stones randomly only on the white sites (or only on the black sites).

Answer: $K=100$ . Suppose Amy places stones only on coordinates $(x,y)$ with $x+y$ odd. Since no two red stones of that type can "attack" each other she can always place on at least half of the total such sites (accounting for Ben's corresponding moves) hence $K \ge \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 200=100$ . Now Ben can partition the board into $4 \times 4$ lattice grids. For any move made by Amy, he simply puts a blue stone symmetric to it in the center of the $4 \times 4$ grid it belongs to; thus guaranteeing $K \le 4 \cdot 25=100$ . As a caveat; we would need to prove that symmetry strategy for Ben on $4 \times 4$ grid always forces Amy to put less than five stones. Let  $a_1$ ,  $a_2$ ,  $\ldots$  be an infinite sequence of positive integers. Suppose that there is an integer  $N > 1$  such that, for each  $n \geq N$ , the number  $$ \frac{a_1}{a_2} + \frac{a_2}{a_3} + \cdots + \frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n} + \frac{a_n}{a_1} $$  is an integer. Prove that there is a positive integer  $M$  such that  $a_m = a_{m+1}$  for all  $m \geq M$ .

*Proposed by Bayarmagnai Gombodorj, Mongolia*
solution_md: The condition implies that the difference $S(n) = rac{a_{n+1}}{a_1} - rac{a_n}{a_1} + rac{a_n}{a_{n+1}}$ is an integer for all $n > N$ . We proceed by $p$ -adic valuation only henceforth.**Claim:** If $p mid a_1$ , then $ u_p(a_{n+1}) \le u_p(a_n)$ for $n \ge N$ . *Proof.* The first two terms of $S(n)$ have nonnegative $ u_p$ , so we need $ u_p( rac{a_n}{a_{n+1}}) \ge 0$ . $ lacksquare$ **Claim:** If $p \mid a_1$ , then $ u_p(a_n)$ is eventually constant. *Proof.* By hypothesis $ u_p(a_1) > 0$ . We consider two cases. - First assume $ u_p(a_k) \ge u_p(a_1)$ for some $k > N$ . We claim that for any $n \ge k$ we have: \[ u_p(a_1) \le u_p(a_{n+1}) \le u_p(a_n). \] This is just by induction on $n$ ; from $ u( rac{a_n}{a_1}) \ge 0$ , we have \[ u_p\left( rac{a_{n+1}}{a_1} + rac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} ight) \ge 0 \] which implies the displayed inequality (since otherwise exactly one term of $S(n)$ has nonnegative $ u_p$ ). Thus once we reach this case, $ u_p(a_n)$ is monotic but bounded below by $ u_p(a_1)$ , and so it is eventually constant. - Now assume $ u_p(a_k) < u_p(a_1)$ for every $k > N$ . Take any $n > N$ then. We have $ u_p\left( rac{a_{n+1}}{a_1} ight) < 0$ , and also $ u_p\left( rac{a_n}{a_1} ight) < 0$ , so among the three terms of $S(n)$ , two must have equal $p$ -adic valuation. We consider all three possibilities: egin{align*} u_p\left( rac{a_{n+1}}{a_1} ight) = u_p\left( rac{a_n}{a_1} ight) &\implies oxed{ u_p(a_{n+1}) = u_p(a_{n})} u_p\left( rac{a_{n+1}}{a_1} ight) = u_p\left( rac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} ight) &\implies oxed{ u_p(a_{n+1}) = rac{ u_p(a_n) + u_p(a_1)}{2}} u_p\left( rac{a_{n}}{a_1} ight) = u_p\left( rac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} ight) &\implies u_p(a_{n+1}) = u_p(a_1), ext{ but this is impossible}. \end{align*} Thus, $ u_p(a_{n+1}) \ge u_p(a_n)$ and $ u_p(a_n)$ is bounded above by $ u_p(a_1)$ . So in this case we must also stabilize. \qedhere $ lacksquare$ Since the latter claim is applied only to finitely many primes, after some time $ u_p(a_n)$ is fixed for all $p \mid a_1$ . Afterwards, the sequence satisfies $a_{n+1} \mid a_n$ for each $n$ , and thus must be eventually constant.**Remark:** This solution is almost completely $p$ -adic, in the sense that I think a similar result if one replaces $a_n \in {\mathbb Z}$ by $a_n \in {\mathbb Z}_p$ for any particular prime $p$ . In other words, the primes almost do not talk to each other. There is one caveat: if $x_n$ is an integer sequence such that $ u_p(x_n)$ is eventually constant for each prime then $x_n$ may not be constant. For example, take $x_n$ to be the $n$ th prime! That's why in the first claim (applied to co-finitely many of the primes), we need the stronger non-decreasing condition, rather than just eventually constant.

Proof by contradiction. For the rest of the solution we assume that the sequence  $a_n$  isn't constant starting from any point. In the end we will achieve a contradiction, thus proving the statement.

The difference  $$  \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_1} + \frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} - \frac{a_n}{a_1} = \frac{a_{n+1}^2 - a_{n+1}a_n + a_na_1}{a_1a_{n+1}}  $$  is an integer for all  $n \ge N$ .**Lemma 1.**
There is a prime  $p$  such that  $v_p(a_{n+1}) \neq v_p(a_n)$  for infinitely many  $n \ge N$ .**Proof.**
The integer-ness condition above implies that  $a_{n+1} \mid a_na_1$ . This means that for all  $p \mid a_n$ ,  $p$  prime and  $n \ge N$ , we have either  $p \mid a_N$  or  $p \mid a_1$  (assume not, and take the smallest  $i > N$  for which  $p \mid a_i$ ). Thus, there are only finitely many  $p$  such that  $p \mid a_n$  for some  $n \ge N$ . Now, for the statement of the lemma, assume not: now, if we take any prime  $p$  which doesn't divide any of the numbers  $a_1, a_N, a_{N+1}, a_{N+2}, \ldots $ , then we of course have  $v_p(a_{n+1}) = v_p(a_n)$  for all  $n \ge N$ . For the rest of the primes, which we have finitely many, we must have  $v_p(a_{n+1}) = v_p(a_n)$  for all large enough  $n$ . But this means that the sequence  $a_n$  is constant, which is a contradiction. Thus, the statement of the lemma is true.

Now, take any prime  $p$  satisfying the condition of lemma 1. Define  $v_p(a_n) = b_n$  for all  $n$ . We aren't that interested in the cases where  $b_{n+1} = b_n$ , but luckily we have infinitely many interesting cases.**Lemma 2.** If  $b_{n+1} > b_n$ , we have  $b_{n+1} = b_1$ .**Proof:** we divide into two cases, one where  $b_{n+1} > b_1$ , and one where  $b_{n+1} < b_1$ . We start by proving a useful lemma.

<u>Lemma</u> Let  $p$  be any prime. Suppose  $x,y,z\in\mathbb{Q}$  with  $\nu_p(x)\le\nu_p(y)\le\nu_p(z)$  and  $\nu_p(x)<0$  and  $x+y+z\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Then,  $\nu_p(x)=\nu_p(y)$ .

<u>Proof of Lemma</u> Suppose instead that  $\nu_p(x)<\nu_p(y),\nu_p(z)$ . Then,
\[x+y+z=p^{\nu_p(x)}\left(\frac{m}{n}+p\frac{r}{s}\right)\]
where  $m,n,s$  are all relatively prime to  $p$ . It is not hard to show that  $\nu_p(m/n+pr/s)=0$ , so we have  $\nu_p(x+y+z)=\nu_p(x)<0$ , so  $x+y+z\not\in\mathbb{Z}$ , a contradiction.  $\blacksquare$ Now to the key claim of the proof.

<u>Claim</u> Let  $p$  be any prime and let  $b_i=\nu_p(a_i)$ . Let  $n$  be the smallest positive integer larger than  $N$  such that  $b_{n+1}>b_n$  (if it exists). Then  $b_{n+1}=b_{n+2}=\cdots$ .

<u>Proof of Claim</u> Note that
\[-\left(\frac{a_1}{a_2}+\frac{a_2}{a_3}+\cdots+\frac{a_{m-1}}{a_m}+\frac{a_m}{a_1}\right)+\left(\frac{a_1}{a_2}+\frac{a_2}{a_3}+\cdots+\frac{a_m}{a_{m+1}}+\frac{a_{m+1}}{a_1}\right)=\frac{a_m}{a_{m+1}}+\frac{a_{m+1}}{a_1}-\frac{a_m}{a_1}\]
is an integer for all positive integers  $m>N$ . Suppose  $m>N$  is a positive integer such that  $b_m<b_{m+1}$ . By the lemma, since  $b_m-b_{m+1}<0$ , one of
\[b_m-b_{m+1},b_{m+1}-b_1,b_m-b_1\]
must be equal to another. We can't have the last two equal to one another, so suppose instead that we had  $b_m-b_{m+1}=b_{m+1}-b_1$ . Then, we see that
\[b_m-b_1=2(b_m-b_{m+1})<b_m-b_{m+1}=b_{m+1}-b_1<0,\]
so by the lemma,  $\frac{a_m}{a_{m+1}}+\frac{a_{m+1}}{a_1}-\frac{a_m}{a_1}$  can't be an integer. Therefore, the only possibility left is that  $b_m-b_{m+1}=b_m-b_1$ , so  $b_{m+1}=b_1$ . Thus whenever the sequence  $\{b_i\}_{i>N}$  strictly increases, it increases to  $b_1$ . This establishes that  $\max\{b_i\}_{i>n}\le b_1$ . Now suppose that  $b_m>b_{m+1}$  for  $m>n$ . Then, we see that
\[b_{m+1}-b_1<b_m-b_1\le 0<b_m-b_{m+1},\]
so we again have a contradiction by the lemma. Therefore, once the sequence increases, it can never decrease, and it also can never increase (since it has to increase to  $b_1$ , but it already is at  $b_1$ ). Thus,  $b_m=b_1$  for all  $m>n$ .  $\blacksquare$ Thus, we see that for each prime  $p$ , the  $b_i$  sequence is eventually constant. If  $p\nmid a_1$ , we can make the stronger statement that the sequence is weakly decreasing after  $n>N$  (after reaching  $N$ , the sequence can never strictly increase, as it would have to increase to  $b_1=0$ , but there is nothing less than  $0$ ). Thus, since there are only finitely many primes dividing  $a_1$ , we see that after some value  $M$ , all the  $b$  sequences are weakly decreasing. This means
\[\cdots a_{M+2}\mid a_{M+1}\mid a_M,\]
which means the sequence is eventually constant.

Take some prime  $p$ . Let  $x_i = \nu_p(a_i)$ . We know  $\nu_p \left(-\frac{a_n}{a_1} + \frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} + \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_1}\right) \ge 0$  for all  $n>N$ . We claim that  $x_{n+1}$  is between  $x_1$  and  $x_n$  for all sufficiently large  $n$  and for all primes  $p$ . 

Case 1:  $x_1 \le x_n$ . We want to show that  $x_1 \le x_{n+1} \le x_n$ . 
If  $\nu_p(a_n/a_1) = \nu_p(a_{n+1}/a_n)$ , then  $x_n = x_{n+1}$ . So  $x_1 \le x_n = x_{n+1}$ , and we are done. 
If   $\nu_p(a_n/a_1) = \nu_p(a_n/a_{n+1})$ , then  $x_{n+1} = x_1$ . But  $x_1 \le x_n$ , so we are done.
If  $\nu_p(a_n/a_{n+1}) = \nu_p(a_{n+1}/a_1)$ , then  $x_{n+1} = \tfrac12( x_n + x_1)$ , so  $x_1 \le x_{n+1} \le x_n$ . 
If none of the above conditions hold, then
\begin{align*}
 0 &\le \nu_p \left(-\frac{a_n}{a_1} + \frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} + \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_1}\right) 
 &= \min(x_n - x_1, x_n - x_{n+1}, x_{n+1}-x_1).
\end{align*}
Then each of the above terms is nonnegative, so 
\[ x_n \ge x_1, x_n \ge x_{n+1}, x_{n+1} \ge x_1 \implies x_{1} \le x_{n+1} \le x_n, \]
as desired. 

Case 2:  $x_n \le x_1$ . Very similar to case 1, just flip the inequality signs. 

Therefore,  $x_{n+1}$  is bounded between  $x_1$  and  $x_n$  for all  $n>N$ . This means that either  $x_n \ge x_1$  for all  $n>N$  or  $x_n \le x_1$  for all  $n>N$ . In the former case,  $(x_i)$  is non-decreasing and bounded above by  $x_1$ , so it is eventually constant. In the latter case,  $(x_i)$  is non-increasing and bounded below by  $x_1$ , so it is eventually constant. Therefore,  $(\nu_p(a_i))$  is eventually constant, for all primes  $p$ , so  $(a_i)$  is eventually constant.

Invert about  $P$  with radius 1, and denote by  $T'$  the image of point  $T$  for any point  $T$ . By the inversion distance formula, we know that  $A'B'=\frac{AB}{PA\cdot PB}$ . As  $P$  lies on  $\omega_{BD}$ , we know that  $\frac{AB}{PA}=\frac{CB}{PC}$ , so  $A'B'=\frac{BC}{PB\cdot PC}=B'C'$ , again by the inversion distance formula. Analogously, we have that  $B'C'=C'D'$  and  $C'D'=D'A'$ , so  $A'B'C'D'$  is a rhombus.

Let us examine what happens with the angle conditions  $\angle XAB=\angle XCD$  and  $\angle XBC=\angle XDA$ . From now on, we use directed angles. By inversion similarity angles, we have that  $\angle XAB=\angle PAB+\angle XAP=\angle A'B'P+\angle PX'A'$  and similarly  $\angle XCD=\angle C'D'P+\angle PX'C'$ , so  $\angle PX'A'-\angle PX'C'=\angle C'D'P-\angle A'B'P$ . The LHS is simply  $\angle C'X'A'$  and the RHS is  $\angle B'PD'$  as  $A'C'\parallel B'D'$ . Thus, we have that  $\angle C'X'A'=\angle B'PD'$  and analogously  $\angle B'X'D'=\angle A'PC'$ .

Now, let us examine what happens with the angle condition we want to prove. So, my friend **[Burii](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/user/100466)** told me about the fact that in an inscribed quadrilateral Brocard point exists if and only if the quadrilateral is harmonic. Then I started playing around with similar configurations and then a miracle happened and the problem was created.
I have actually found my old notes that led me to this problem. The story is the following: I wanted to prove that if $X$ is a Brocard point in a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ then $ABCD$ is harmonic. I came up with the following proof:
Let $\angle XAB = \angle XBC = \angle XCD = \angle XDA = \xi$ . Angle chasing gives \begin{align*} \angle BXA + \angle DXC &= (\pi - \xi - \angle ABX) + (\pi - \xi - \angle CDX) & = 2\pi - (\angle ABX + \xi) - (\angle CDX + \xi) & = 2\pi - \angle ABC - \angle CDA & = \pi. \end{align*} So let us consider a point $P$ such that $\triangle XCD \sim \triangle XPA$ . Then $P$ lies on $BX$ as $\angle AXP + \angle BXA = \angle DXC + \angle BXA = \pi$ . Since $\angle XPA = \angle XCD = \xi = \angle XAB$ , we have $\triangle BXA \sim \triangle BAP$ . Using these similarities we get $$ \frac{CD}{DX} = \frac{PA}{AX} = \frac{BP}{BA} \qquad \text{ and } \qquad \frac{CX}{DX} = \frac{PX}{AX} $$ Therefore \begin{align*} AB \cdot CD &= BP \cdot DX & = (PX + BX) \cdot DX & = PX \cdot DX + BX \cdot DX & = AX \cdot CX + BX \cdot DX. \end{align*} Analogously $BC \cdot DA = AX \cdot CX + BX \cdot DX$ , so $AB\cdot CD = BC \cdot AD$ .
I noticed that I used the equalities $\angle XAB = \angle XBC = \angle XCD = \angle XDA$ in order to prove that $\angle AXB + \angle CXD = \pi$ . Later on I used $\angle XAB = \angle XCD$ and $\angle XBC = \angle XDA$ separately. This leads to the following proposition:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. Let $X$ be in the interior of $ABCD$ such that $\angle XAB = \angle XCD$ and $\angle XBC = \angle XDA$ . Suppose that $\angle AXB + \angle CXD = \pi$ . Then $AB \cdot CD = BC \cdot DA$ .
I contemplated the converse. It turned out to be true and much harder than the original proposition. So this is how the problem was created.

I am going to give a partial attempt at a projective generalisation to this problem. Also, some thoughts and motivation along the way. The reason this problem is quite difficult is because the problem is phrased in a Euclidean, where it seems that it should naturally lie as a problem in Projective geometry. Let me elaborate on this: The point $X$ satisfies the property that the angle bisectors of $\{XA, XC\}, \{XB, XD\}, \{XE, XF\}$ are the same, and they are the centres of the involution swapping these lines. This can be shown using Desargues Involution Theorem. We seek such points $X$ . Here is a curious projective result. **Lemma:**Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic, and let the centre be $O$ and a focus be $F_1$ . Take two points $A, C$ on $\mathcal{C}$ and take a point $B$ on $OF_1$ . Take the polar of $B$ w.r.t. $\mathcal{C}$ and intersect this polar with $OF$ to make the point $D$ (a sort of inversion, which we will just call the inverse). Then $A'B'=\frac{AB}{PA\times PB}$ . *Proof:* We have $\bigtriangleup PAB\sim\bigtriangleup PB'A'$ so $$ \frac{A'B'}{AB}=\frac{PB'}{PA}=\frac{1}{PB\times PA} $$ Using Lemma 1, we have $$ A'B'\times C'D'=\frac{AB}{XA\times XB}\times\frac{CD}{XC\times CD}=\frac{BC}{XB\times XC}\times\frac{DA}{XD\times XA}=B'C'\times D'A' $$ **Lemma 2:** $ABCD\sim D'A'B'C'$ . Consider the set $S$ of quadrilaterals $WXYZ$ such that angles $W,X,Y,Z$ are equal to $A,B,C,D$ and $D',A',B',C'$ respectively and $XY=A'B'$ . Then place $WXYZ$ such that $WXYZ$ and $D'A'B'C'$ overlap with each other with $XY$ on $A'B'$ . We now fix the position of $XY=A'B'$ and we vary $W,Z$ on rays $A'D'$ and $B'C'$ respectively. We notice that this covers all quadrilaterals $WXYZ$ in $S$ , and in particular, the value of $XY\times WZ$ is strictly increasing at a slower rate than $WX\times YZ$ as $W,Z$ go further away from $XY$ . Then there exists exactly one quadrilateral $WXYZ$ with $WX\times YZ=XY\times ZW$ and we notice that if $WXYZ$ is similar to $ABCD$ this is attained. But we know $D'A'\times B'C'=A'B'\times C'D'$ , so $D'A'B'C'$ is this quadrilateral, so it is indeed similar to $ABCD$ . **Finishing:** We prove $\frac{AB}{CD}=\frac{XB}{XD}$ and $\frac{BC}{DA}=\frac{XC}{XA}$ . *Proof:* Now, using Lemmas 1 and 2, we have $ABCD\sim D'A'B'C'$ so $$ \frac{AB}{BC}=\frac{D'A'}{A'B'}=\frac{DA}{XD\times XA}\div\frac{AB}{XA\times XB}=\frac{DA}{AB}\times\frac{XB}{XD} $$ so we have $$ \frac{XB}{XD}=\frac{AB^2}{BC\times DA}=\frac{AB^2}{AB\times CD}=\frac{AB}{CD} $$ and similarly $\frac{BC}{DA}=\frac{XC}{XA}$ . Then by Law of Sines, we have $$ \frac{\sin{\angle AXB}}{\sin{\angle XAB}}=\frac{AB}{XB}=\frac{CD}{XD}=\frac{\sin{\angle CXD}}{\sin{\angle XCD}} $$ so $\sin{\angle AXB}=\sin{\angle CXD}$ and by symmetry, $\sin{\angle BXC}=\sin{\angle DXA}$ . Then if $\angle AXB+\angle CXD\neq 180^{\circ}$ , then $\angle AXB=\angle CXD\neq 90^{\circ}$ which would imply $\angle BXC=\angle DXA=180^{\circ}-\angle AXB$ so $B,X,D$ and $A,X,C$ are collinear. Then $ABCD$ is a parallelogram, but $AB\times CD=BC\times DA$ implies that $ABCD$ is a rhombus, so the conclusion follows similarly.

This is true by a ratio chase: if the isogonal line at $C$ meets $\overline{BD}$ at $X_2'$ and the isogonal line at $A$ meets $\overline{BD}$ at $X_2''$ , then \[\frac{AB^2}{BP \cdot BX_2''} =\frac{AD^2}{DP \cdot DX_2''} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{BC^2}{BP \cdot BX_2'} = \frac{CD^2}{DP \cdot DX_2'}.\] But since $\tfrac{AB^2}{BC^2} = \tfrac{AD^2}{CD^2}$ , dividing yields $\tfrac{BX_2''}{DX_2''} = \tfrac{BX_2'}{DX_2'}$ , i.e. $X_2'' = X_2'$ . $\blacksquare$ Then the circles $(ADX_1) \cap (BCX_1) \cap (ABX_2) \cap (BCX_2)$ concur as $X_1$ and $X_2$ are Clawson-Schmidt conjugates. Say they concur at $X'$ ; then $\measuredangle BAX' = \measuredangle BX_1X' = \measuredangle DX_1'X' = \measuredangle DCX'$ and similar. So actually $X = X'$ . It follows that $\angle BXA + \angle CXD = \angle BX_1A +\angle CX_1D = 180^\circ$ because $X_1$ has an isogonal conjugate, namely $X_2$ . This finishes the proof.

Thank you for this beautiful inequality v_enhance! We claim that the maximum value of the given expression is $\boxed{\frac{8}{\sqrt[3]{7}}}$ which is attained for $(a, b, c, d) = (49, 1, 49, 1)$ . Here's my proof (similar to many other proofs mention above) : We see that if $T[x, y] = \sqrt[3]{\frac{x}{y+7}}$ . We see that $T[x, y] + T[y, x] \leq T[x+y+14, 0]$ by completing Hölder's inequality on $(x + 7)(7 + y)((x+7)+ (y+7))$ . Now, for the final showdown, observe that $T[a, b] + T[b, c] + T[c, d] + T[d, a] \leq T[a', d'] + T[d', a'] + T[b', c'] + T[c', b']$ by using Rearrangement inequality on the descending sequences $\left \langle \sqrt[3]{a'} \right \rangle$ and $\left \langle \sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{d'+7}} \right \rangle$ ( $a', b', c', d'$ is a permutation of $a, b, c, d$ but in increasing order). and hence we get that $T[a, b] + T[b, c] + T[c, d] + T[d, a] \leq [T, a' + d' +14, 0] + T[b' + c' + 14, 0] \leq$ $ \underset{\mathrm{simple inequality}}{\underline{\sqrt[3]{4\frac{a'+b'+c'+d'}{7}}}} = \boxed{\frac{8}{\sqrt[3]{7}}}$ as desired.

<details><summary>My solution</summary>The answer is  $8/\sqrt[3]{7}$ , obtained when  $(a, b, c, d) = (1, 49, 1, 49)$ . We now prove that this is the best possible.**Lemma.** [Two-variable version] For all nonnegative real  $x$  and  $y$ ,
\[
    \sqrt[3]{\frac{x}{y+7}} +
    \sqrt[3]{\frac{y}{x+7}}
    \le \sqrt[3]{\frac{x+y}{7} + 2}.
\]
*Proof.* Apply Hölder inequality as
\[(x+7)(7+y)\big((x+7) + (y+7)\big)
\ge \left(\sqrt[3]{7x(x+7)} + \sqrt[3]{7y(y+7)}\right)^3,\]
which is equivalent to the desired inequality.  $\square$ Returning to the problem, let  $x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4$  denote the increasing permutation of  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$ ,  $d$ . Then by rearrangement inequality,
\[
	\sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt[3]{\frac{a}{b+7}}
	\le \sum_{i + j = 5} \sqrt[3]{\frac{x_i}{x_j + 7}}.
\]
By the lemma, the RHS above is at most
\[
	\sqrt[3]{\frac{x_1 + x_4}{7} + 2} +
	\sqrt[3]{\frac{x_2 + x_3}{7} + 2}
	\le 2 \sqrt[3]{\frac{50}{7} + 2}
	= \frac{8}{\sqrt[3]{7}}
\]
since  $\sqrt[3]{\bullet}$  is concave on the positive reals.</details>

Let  $S$  be the desired quantity. The answer is \[ S \le \frac{8}{\sqrt[3]{7}} 	\quad \text{ achieved when } \quad 	(a,b,c,d) = (49, 1, 49, 1).  \] We present three solutions for the upper bound.

Set  $a = w^2$ ,  $b = x^2$ ,  $c = y^2$ ,  $d = z^2$  and moreover define  $t = w+x+y+z$ . First, by H\"older inequality we have \[ S^3 \le \left( \sum_{\text{cyc}} w \right) 	\left( \sum_{\text{cyc}} w \right) 	\left( \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{1}{x^2+7} \right). \] Also, we use will use the key estimate \begin{align*} 	0 &\le \frac{(x-1)^2 (x-7)^2}{x^2+7}  	&= x^2-16x+71 - \frac{448}{x^2+7}  	\implies \frac{1}{x^2+7} &\le \frac{x^2-16x+71}{448}  	\implies \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{1}{x^2+7} 	&\le \sum_{\text{cyc}}  \frac{x^2-16x+71}{448} 		= \frac{6}{7} - \frac{t}{28} \end{align*} Consequently, the earlier estimate gives \[ 	S^3 \le \frac{t^2(24-t)}{28} 	= \frac{t \cdot t \cdot (48-2t)}{56} 	\le \frac{16^3}{56} = \frac{512}{7} \] as desired, with the last inequality by AM-GM.

For notation purposes let \((a,b,c,d)\) be that expression. First of all, by re-arrangement the proposed inequality for \((a,b,c,d)\) is true if it is true for \((b,a,d,c)\). So, if \(S\) is the maximum of \[(a,b,c,d)+(b,a,d,c)\] then our desired answer will be \(\frac{S}{2}\). Now this triggers us to find the upper bound of \[\sqrt[3]{\frac{a}{b+7}}+\sqrt[3]{\frac{b}{a+7}}\] in terms of \(a\) and \(b\). Now the inequality that will ring a bell is Holder, because of the cube root and moreover we want to change this disgusting fractional form into something nice and linear. With that motive, we consider \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{a+7}}\) to be a part of the holder inequality, that is \[\sqrt[3]{7}\sqrt[3]{b}\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{a+7}}+\sqrt[3]{a}\sqrt[3]{7}\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{b+7}}\leq \sqrt[3]{(7+a)(7+b)\left(\frac{1}{a+7}+\frac{1}{b+7}\right)}=\sqrt[3]{a+b+14}\] and this seems pretty cute. Now, we need the maximum of \[\sqrt[3]{a+b+14}+\sqrt[3]{b+c+14}+\sqrt[3]{c+d+14}+\sqrt[3]{d+a+14}\] and by holder, it is just \[\sqrt[3]{16(a+b+c+d+a+b+c+d+56)}=\sqrt[3]{2^{12}}=16\] implying that \(S=\frac{16}{\sqrt[3]{7}}\) and so, our desired answer is \(\frac{S}{2}=\frac{8}{\sqrt[3]{7}}\). Now to find the equality, we need \(a=c\) and \(b=d\) and \(a+b=50\). So we need \[\sqrt[3]{\frac{a}{b+7}}+\sqrt[3]{\frac{b}{a+7}}=\frac{4}{\sqrt[3]{7}}\] and also \(a+b=50\), so \[\sqrt[3]{\frac{50-a}{a+7}}+\sqrt[3]{\frac{a}{57-a}}=\frac{4}{\sqrt[3]{7}}\] Clearly \(a+7\) or \(57-a\) should be a multiple of \(7\), for \(a+7\) we try \(a=0\), and we don't get equality case, for \(57-a\), we try \(a=1\) which indeed gives us the equality case, so the answer is \((49,1,49,1)\) and by symmetry \(a=49\) works too. Now to prove that this is the only possible case, we can consider the graph of the function \[\sqrt[3]{\frac{a}{b+7}}+\sqrt[3]{\frac{b}{a+7}}=\frac{4}{\sqrt[3]{7}}\] and verify that it intersects the graph in only two possible real points, which are \(1\) and \(49\).

stem_md:
Let  $n>1$  be a positive integer. Each cell of an  $n\times n$  table contains an integer. Suppose that the following conditions are satisfied:
[list=1]
[*] Each number in the table is congruent to  $1$  modulo  $n$ .
[*] The sum of numbers in any row, as well as the sum of numbers in any column, is congruent to  $n$  modulo  $n^2$ .
[/list]
Let  $R_i$  be the product of the numbers in the  $i^{\text{th}}$  row, and  $C_j$  be the product of the number in the  $j^{\text{th}}$  column. Prove that the sums  $R_1+\hdots R_n$  and  $C_1+\hdots C_n$  are congruent modulo  $n^4$ .
solution_md: Notice that the only possible residues for an element of the table mod $n^2$ are $an+1$ for $0\le a\le n-1$ . For every integer in the grid, if it is equal to $an+1 \pmod {n^2}$ for $1\le a\le n-1$ , call $a$ the *label* of that integer. Take labels mod $n$ , so that a label of $a+n$ is the same as a label of $a$ . As the sum of the numbers in any row or column is equal to $n \pmod {n^2}$ , the sum of the labels of all integers in any row and column is equivalent to $0$ mod $n$ .**Claim:** Changing an integer by an integer multiple of $n^2$ does not change the difference between $R_1+\ldots+R_n$ and $C_1+\ldots+C_n$ mod $n^4$ . *Proof.* WLOG let the integer changed be in the first row and first column, and have label $x$ . Then we need to prove that $R_1$ and $C_1$ get changed by the same amount mod $n^4$ . $R_1$ gets changed by a multiple of $n^2$ multiplied by the product of the remainder of numbers in the row. It suffices to consider the product of the remainder of the numbers mod $n^2$ . If there are two numbers with labels $a$ and $b$ , their product is congruent to $$ (an+1)(bn+1)\equiv (a+b)n+1 $$ mod $n^2$ , and therefore their product is $1$ mod $n$ and has a label of $a+b$ . Thus, if all the remaining numbers in the first row were multiplied, the product mod $n^2$ would have a label equal to the sum of the labels of all such integers, which is equal to $-x$ . Therefore the change in $R_1$ is equivalent to $(-xn+1)(cn^2)$ mod $n^4$ for some $c$ . However, using the same reasoning for $C_1$ , we are done. $\blacksquare$ Thus, we can assume that all numbers are between $0$ and $n^2$ , and so every label $a$ mod $n$ corresponds to a unique number $an+1$ . It is well-known that if we are given labels for the numbers in the top left $(n-1)\times (n-1)$ subsquare, we can uniquely fill out labels for the rest of the entries in the grid so that in every row and column the sum of the labels is $0$ mod $n$ . Thus it suffices to prove that for any set of labels we can put in the $(n-1)\times (n-1)$ subsquare, the resulting grid has the desired property. We will use induction on the sum of the remainders of the labels mod $n$ in the subsquare. The base case, where this quantity is $0$ , only occurs when the labels in the subsquare are all $0$ , creating a grid of only labels $0$ , corresponding to a grid of all $1$ , which clearly has the desired property. The inductive step will be proven by the following claim. **Claim:** If $1$ is added to a label of an integer in the subsquare, then the difference between $R_1+\ldots+R_n$ and $C_1+\ldots+C_n$ does not change mod $n^4$ . *Proof.*WLOG assume that number is in the first row and first column again, having original label $a$ . Then the only changes in the resulting grid is that $1$ is subtracted from the labels in the $n$ column of the first row (having original label $b$ ), and the first column of the $n$ th row (having original label $c$ ), as well as adding $1$ to the label of the integer in the $n$ th column and the $n$ th row (having original label $d$ ). Thus, only $R_1,R_n,C_1,C_n$ will change. $R_1$ will change by the change in product of the two entries changed multiplied by the product of the unchanged integers in the first row. The change in product of the two entries changed is equal to $$ ((a+1)n+1)((b-1)n+1)-(an+1)(bn+1)=n^2(-a+b-1). $$ Thus, it suffices to find the product of the unchanged elements in the first row mod $n^2$ , by the reasoning in the first claim, as the sum of the labels of all such integers is equal to $-a-b$ , this is equal to $n(-a-b)+1$ . Thus the change in $R_1$ mod $n^4$ is equal to $n^2(-a+b-1)(n(-a-b)+1)$ . Similarly, the change in $R_n$ is equal to $n^2(-d+c-1)(n(-c-d)+1)$ , the change in $C_1$ is $n^2(-a+c-1)(n(-a-c)+1)$ , and the change in $C_n$ is $n^2(-d+b-1)(n(-b-d)+1)$ . We can ignore the factor of $n^2$ because it appears in every change. It is straightforward to check that $(-a+b-1)(n(-a-b)+1)+(-d+c-1)(n(-c-d)+1)$ and $(-a+c-1)(n(-a-c)+1)+(-d+b-1)(n(-b-d)+1)$ are both equal to $$ -2-a+b+c-d+(a+b+c+d)n-na^2+nb^2+nc^2-nd^2, $$ and thus the claim is proven. $\blacksquare$ This claim proves the inductive step because it shows for a particular set of labels, subtracting one from a label does not change the difference between $R_1+\ldots+R_n$ and $C_1+\ldots+C_n$ mod $n^4$ , implying we can use the induction hypothesis to finish. We are done.

We present two solutions: first, a sort of mechanical approach which reveals some underlying traps in the problem, and a second elegant approach that hides them. **First solution by brute force (mine)** We denote the numbers in the grid by $1 + na_{i,j}$ in the obvious way, meaning that the given states that $n$ divides $a_{i,1} + \dots + a_{i,n}$ and $a_{1,j} + \dots + a_{n,j}$ for any $i$ or $j$ . In what follows, I'm going to take be actually working with addition modulo $1$ : write $a \equiv b \pmod 1$ if $a-b \in {\mathbb Z}$ . (This works fine as long as we are careful to not multiply.) Our goal is to show that $\frac{\sum_i R_i - \sum_j C_j}{n^4} \equiv 0 \pmod 1$ . We begin by computing $R_i$ carefully. Let \[ r_i(k) \overset{\text{def}}{=} a_{i,1}^k + \dots + a_{i,n}^k \] denote the sum of the $k$ th powers in the $n$ th row, which we are given is divisible by $n$ . Then we compute $R_i$ in terms of $r_i(k)$ for $k \le 3$ : \begin{align*} \frac{R_i}{n^4} &= \frac{1}{n^4} \prod_j \left( 1 + n a_{i,j} \right) &\equiv \frac{1 + n\sum_j a_{i,j} + n^2 \sum_{j_1 < j_2} a_{i,j_1} a_{i,j_2} + n^3 \sum_{j_1 < j_2 < j_3} a_{i,j_1} a_{i,j_2} a_{i,j_3}}{n^4} \pmod 1 &= \frac{1}{n^4} + \frac{r_i(1)}{n^3} + \frac{r_i(1)^2-r_i(2)}{2n^2} + \frac{2r_i(3) + r_i(1)^3 - 3r_i(1)r_i(2)}{6n} &= \frac{1+nr_i(1) - \frac{1}{2} n^2 r_i(2) + \frac13 n^3 r_i(3)}{n^4} + \frac{r_i(1)^2}{2n^2} + \frac{r_i(1)^3}{6n} - \frac{r_i(1)r_i(2)}{2n}. \end{align*} However, \[ \sum_i \left[ 1+nr_i(1) - \frac{1}{2} n^2 r_i(2) + \frac13 n^3 r_i(3) \right] = n + \sum_{i,j} \left[ na_{i,j} - \frac{1}{2} n^2 a_{i,j}^2 + \frac 13 n^3 a_{i,j}^3 \right] \] which is symmetric with respect to rows and columns. So if we define $c_j(k)$ in an analogous way, and compute $\frac{1}{n^4}( \sum_i R_i - \sum_j C_j)$ , the first fraction cancels entirely and we get \begin{align*} \frac{\sum_i R_i - \sum_j C_j}{n^4} &\equiv \frac{\sum_i r_i(1)^3 - \sum_j c_j(1)^3}{6n} - \frac{\sum_i r_i(1) r_i(2) - \sum_j c_j(1) c_j(2)}{2n} &\phantom{\equiv} + \frac{\sum_i r_i(1)^2 - \sum_j c_j(1)^2}{2n^2} \pmod 1 &\equiv \frac{\sum_i r_i(1)^3 - \sum_j c_j(1)^3}{6n} - \frac{\sum_i r_i(1)^2 - \sum_j c_j(1)^2}{2n} &\phantom{\equiv} + \frac{\sum_i r_i(1)^2 - \sum_j c_j(1)^2}{2n^2} \pmod 1 \end{align*} where the last line is since $r_i(2) \equiv r_i(1) \pmod 2$ , thus $r_i(1) r_i(2) \equiv r_i(1)^2 \pmod{2n}$ . We wish to show the right-hand side is an integer. In fact, we claim all three fractions above are integers. To do this, it is enough to check:**Claim:** Let $p$ be a prime which divides $n$ . Then the $\nu_p(\cdot)$ of each of the three fractions is positive. *Proof.* For the first fraction, we have \[ \nu_p\left( r_i(1)^3 \right) = 3\nu_p(n) \ge \nu_p(6n) \] and similarly for $c_j(1)^3$ , which implies the result for the first fraction (since we assumed $\nu_p(n) > 0$ ). The proof for the second fraction is the same. For the final fraction, the result is obvious for $p>2$ . For $p=2$ we note that $\sum_i r_i(1) = \sum_j c_j(1)$ , and hence the number of terms on each side with exponent of $2$ equal to $\nu_2(n)$ (the minimum possible) must be equal mod $2$ . So among the $2n$ terms of $\sum_i r_i(1)^2 - \sum_j c_j(1)^2$ , the number of terms with $2$ -adic exponent $2\nu_2(n)$ is even, and hence together those terms are divisible by $2n^2$ . The rest of the terms are divisible by $4n^2$ , so the result follows. $\blacksquare$ Since the left-hand side is in $\frac{1}{n^4}{\mathbb Z}$ it follows the expression is an integer, as desired.**Remark:** I thought this solution is direct, but there is a big pitfall with division buried inside this approach, which is why the argument looks so convoluted later on. It might be tempting to try to write \[ R_i \equiv 1 + n r_i(1) + n^2 \cdot \frac{r_i(1)^2-r_i(2)}{2} + n^3 \cdot \frac{r_i(1)^3 + 2r_i(3) - 3r_i(1)r_i(2) }{3} \pmod{n^4} \] and finish directly by appealing to the fact that $r_i(1) \equiv 0 \pmod n$ to eliminate all but the isolated terms that cancelled earlier. This would indeed work if $\gcd(n,6) = 1$ . However, when $\gcd(n,6) \neq 1$ , one runs into trouble with the denominators above: it is no longer true that $n^2 \cdot \frac{r_i(1)^2}{2} \equiv 0 \pmod{n^4}$ , for example, and significant care must be taken. That is why the argument is written in the less natural ``mod $1$ '' framework, to emphasize that we are not doing the usual modular arithmetic (and accordingly to keep readers on appropriate guard). **Second trickier approach (official solution)** Again denote the numbers by $1 + na_{i,j}$ in the obvious way. Let $P = \prod_i \prod_j (1 + na_{i,j})$ . We will show that \[ \sum_i R_i \equiv (n-1) + P \pmod{n^4} \] which will imply the result. First, note that $R_i \equiv 1 \pmod{n^2}$ for any $i$ . This follows from an excerpt of the calculation in Solution 1; one notes $\prod_j (1+na_{i,j}) \equiv 1 + n(a_{i,1} + \dots + a_{i,n}) \equiv 1 \pmod{n^2}$ . Then, \begin{align*} P &= \prod_i R_i = \prod_i \left( 1 + (R_i-1) \right) & \equiv 1 + \sum_i (R_i-1) \equiv -(n-1) + \sum_i R_i \pmod{n^4}. \end{align*} since the product of any two terms of the form $R_i-1$ is divisible by $n^2 \cdot n^2 = n^4$ . End proof.

Another brute force solution

First, we will abuse the sigma notations. Let  $\sum a_i$  denotes  $\sum\limits_{i=1}^n a_i$ ,  $\sum a_ia_j$  denotes  $\sum\limits_{1\leqslant i < j\leqslant n} a_ia_j$  and  $\sum a_ia_ja_k$  denotes  $\sum\limits_{1\leqslant i < j < k\leqslant n} a_ia_ja_k$ .**Claim:** Let a row has entries  $r_i=a_in+1$  ( $i=1,2,...,n$ ). Then  $$ r_1r_2...r_n \equiv \frac{n^3}{3}\sum a_i^3 - \frac{n^2}{2}\sum a_i^2 + \left(\frac{n^3}{2}+n\right)\sum a_i + 1 \pmod{n^4} $$  **Proof:** The given conditions imply  $n\mid a_1+a_2+...+a_n$ . Clearly,  $$ r_1r_2...r_n\equiv n^3\sum a_ia_ja_k + n^2\sum a_ia_j + n\sum a_i + 1\pmod{n^4}. $$  Now we recall the following identities,
\begin{align*}
\sum a_ia_j &= \frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\sum a_i\right)^2 - \sum a_i^2\right] 
\sum a_ia_ja_k &= \frac{1}{6}\left[\left(\sum a_i\right)^3
- 3\left(\sum a_i^2\right)\left(\sum a_i\right)
+ 2\left(\sum a_i^3\right)\right].
\end{align*}
By collecting massive amount of terms, it suffices to show that  $$ \frac{n^3}{6}\left(\sum a_i\right)^3
- \frac{n^3}{2}\left(\sum a_i^2\right)\left(\sum a_i\right)
+ \frac{n^2}{2}\left(\sum a_i\right)^3
- \frac{n^3}{2}\sum a_i \equiv 0\pmod{n^4} $$  We take care of the last two first. These terms combined are equal to  $$ n^4\times \frac{K^2-K}{2} \equiv 0\pmod{n^4} $$  where  $K=\dfrac{\sum a_i}{n}$ . For the first two, note that
\begin{align*}
\frac{n^3}{6}\left(\sum a_i\right)^3
&= n^4 \cdot  K^3 \cdot \frac{n^2}{6} 
\frac{n^3}{2}\left(\sum a_i^2\right)\left(\sum a_i\right) &= n^4 \cdot K \cdot \frac{\sum a_i^2}{2}
\end{align*}
Since  $\gcd(n^4,6)$  always divide  $n^2$ , linear congruence  $6x\equiv n^2\pmod{n^4}$  always have the solution which means the first term is always  $\equiv 0\pmod n$ . 

Moreover, if  $2\mid n$  then  $2\mid\sum a_i^2$ , otherwise  $2^{-1}$  exists in  $\pmod{n^4}$ . Thus the second term is  $\equiv 0\pmod n$  as well. Hence we are done.

The problem is now easily solved by just summing the claim over all rows and all columns.

\[\sum_{r \in R} \prod_{a_i \in r} (a_i+1) \equiv \sum_{c \in C} \prod_{a_j \in c} (a_j+1) \pmod{n^4}\]
(Note: I will use  $\sum_R$  to sum over all rows, where the  $a_i$  within the sum are the numbers in a particular row. I also get a little lazy with indexing, oops.)
\[\iff \sum_{R} \left(\sum_{1 \le i <j \le n} a_ia_j + \sum_{1 \le i < j < k \le n} a_ia_ja_k \right) \equiv \sum_{C} \left(\sum_{1 \le i <j \le n} a_ia_j + \sum_{1 \le i < j < k \le n} a_ia_ja_k \right) \pmod{n^4}.\]
Divide each number in the grid by  $n$  and note that for each  $i$  we have  $R_i = \sum_{a \in r_i}a \equiv 0 \pmod n$  and similarly  $C_i \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$  for columns. The desired congruence is equivalent to
\[\sum_{R} \sum a_ia_j +\sum_{R} n\sum a_ia_ja_k \equiv \sum_{C} \sum a_ia_j + \sum_{C}n\sum a_ia_ja_k \pmod{n^2}. \quad (\heartsuit)\]

\[ S := \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{a=1}^n \sum_{b>a} y_{ia}y_{ib} \pmod{n^2}\]

We denote the numbers in the table by \( n a_{ij} + 1 \) for \( i,j = 1,2,\dots,n \).
Then, for each row,
\[R_i = (n a_{i1} + 1)(n a_{i2} + 1)\cdots (n a_{in} + 1)
 = 1 + n(a_{i1} + a_{i2} + \cdots + a_{in}) \equiv 1 \pmod{n^2}.\]
Now consider the product of all \( n^2 \) numbers, and denote it by \( P \).
\[P = R_1 R_2 \cdots R_n = (1 + (R_1 - 1))(1 + (R_2 - 1)) \cdots (1 + (R_n - 1)).\]
Expanding this expression and noting that\[(R_i - 1)(R_j - 1) \equiv 0 \pmod{n^4},\]
we obtain\[P \equiv 1 + (R_1 - 1) + (R_2 - 1) + \cdots + (R_n - 1) \pmod{n^4}.\]
Therefore,\[P + n - 1 \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n} R_i \pmod{n^4}.\]
Since the left-hand side of this congruence depends only on the initial table configuration,  
we can analogously repeat the same reasoning for the column products \( C_j \), yielding

The word "grid" will refer to grids satisfying the two conditions.

Call a grid *good* if the sum of the products of the numbers in each row is equal to the sum of the products of the numbers in each column. Let  $a_{i,\,j}$  be the number in the cell  $(i,\,j)$ .**Lemma 1.** Increasing any entry of a good grid by  $n^2$  yields a good grid.
*Proof.* Permute the rows and columns so WLOG  $a_{1,\,1}$  is increased by  $n^2$ . Let  $a_{i,\,j}=:1+nb_{i,\,j}$ , so the sum of  $b_{i,\,j}$  across any row or column is  $0$  mod  $n$ . The product of the numbers in the affected row  $1$  increases by
\[
n^2\prod_{k=2}^n(1+nb_{1,\,k})\equiv n^2\left(1+n\sum_{k=2}^nb_{1,\,k}\right)\equiv n^2(1-nb_{1,\,1})\pmod{n^4}.
\]
This is symmetric in rows and columns, so the product of the numbers in the affected column  $1$  increases by the same amount.  $\square$ **Corollary 2.** Two grids which are congruent mod  $n^2$  are either both good or both bad.

Let  $G$  be a grid with entries  $a_{i,\,j}$  and let  $G'$  be a grid with entries  $a_{i,\,j}'$ .  $G$  and  $G'$  are said to be *similar* if there exist integers  $i_1,\,i_2,\,j_1,\,j_2,\,k$  such that
\begin{align*}
a_{i_1,\,j_1}'&=a_{i_1,\,j_1}+kn
a_{i_1,\,j_2}'&=a_{i_1,\,j_2}-kn
a_{i_2,\,j_1}'&=a_{i_2,\,j_1}-kn
a_{i_2,\,j_2}'&=a_{i_2,\,j_2}+kn
\end{align*}
and  $a_{i,\,j}=a_{i,\,j}'$  for all other  $(i,\,j)$ .**Lemma 3.** Two similar grids are either both good or both bad.
*Proof.* Suppose the two grids have entries  $a_{i,\,j}$  and  $a_{i,\,j}'$ . Permute the rows so WLOG there exists an integer  $k$  such that
\begin{align*}
a_{1,\,1}'&=a_{1,\,1}+kn
a_{1,\,2}'&=a_{1,\,2}-kn
a_{2,\,1}'&=a_{2,\,1}-kn
a_{2,\,2}'&=a_{2,\,2}+kn
\end{align*}
and  $a_{i,\,j}=a_{i,\,j}'$  for all other  $(i,\,j)$ . Let  $a_{i,\,j}=:1+nb_{i,\,j}$ . Note that only rows and columns  $1$  and  $2$  are affected. Since  $a_{1,\,1}'a_{1,\,2}'=a_{1,\,1}a_{1,\,2}+kn^2(b_{1,\,2}-b_{1,\,1})-k^2n^2$ , the product of the numbers in row  $1$  increases by
\begin{align*}
n^2(k(b_{1,\,2}-b_{1,\,1})-k^2)\prod_{k=3}^n(1+nb_{1,\,k})&\equiv n^2(k(b_{1,\,2}-b_{1,\,1})-k^2)\left(1+n\sum_{k=3}^n b_{1,\,k}\right)
&\equiv n^2(k(b_{1,\,2}-b_{1,\,1})-k^2)(1-n(b_{1,\,2}+b_{1,\,1}))\pmod{n^4}.
\end{align*}
Similarly, the product of the numbers in row  $2$  increases by  $n^2(k(b_{2,\,1}-b_{2,\,2})-k^2)(1-n(b_{2,\,1}+b_{2,\,2}))$  mod  $n^4$ . Hence the value of  $R_1+\cdots+R_n$  increases by
\begin{align*}
&\quad\,\ n^2(k(b_{1,\,2}-b_{1,\,1})-k^2)(1-n(b_{1,\,2}+b_{1,\,1}))+n^2(k(b_{2,\,1}-b_{2,\,2})-k^2)(1-n(b_{2,\,1}+b_{2,\,2}))
&=n^2\left(k(b_{1,\,2}+b_{2,\,1}-b_{1,\,1}-b_{2,\,2})-2k^2\right)+k^2n^3(b_{1,\,1}+b_{2,\,2}+b_{1,\,2}+b_{2,\,1})-kn^3(b_{1,\,2}^2+b_{2,\,1}^2-b_{1,\,1}^2-b_{2,\,2}^2)
\end{align*}
mod  $n^4$ . Since this is symmetric in rows and columns,  $C_1+\cdots+C_n$  increases by the same amount.  $\square$ **Claim 4.** For any grid  $G$ , there exists a sequence  $G=G_0,\,G_1,\,\ldots,\,G_m$  such that  $G_i$  and  $G_{i+1}$  are similar for all  $0\leq i\leq m-1$ , and  $G_m$  is a grid consisting of only  $1$ 's mod  $n^2$ .
*Proof.* For each cell  $a_{i,\,j}$  with  $i,\,j\leq n-1$ , subtract  $a_{i,\,j}-1$  from  $a_{i,\,j}$  and  $a_{n,\,n}$ , and add  $a_{i,\,j}-1$  to  $a_{i,\,n}$  and  $a_{n,\,j}$  to get a new grid. We end up with a sequence where adjacent terms are similar and the last term has  $a_{i,\,j}=1$  for all  $i,\,j\leq n-1$ . By condition 2, it follows that  $a_{i,\,n}$  and  $a_{n,\,i}$  are also  $1$  mod  $n^2$  for all  $1\leq i\leq n$ , as desired.  $\square$ Since the grid containing only  $1$ 's is good,  $G_m$  is good by Corollary 2. Thus  $G$  is good by Lemma 3.  $\square$

stem_md: Determine all functions  $f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$  satisfying   $$ \left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)f(y)=f(xy)+f\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) $$   for all  $x,y>0$ .
solution_md:
The answer is  $\boxed{f(x)=ax+\tfrac bx}$  for real numbers  $a$  and  $b$ . It is easy to check that this works; so it suffices to prove that these are the only solutions.

Let  $P(x,y)$  denote the assertion. Notice that if  $f$  and  $g$  are solutions to the functional equation,  $f+g$  and  $f-g$  are also solutions. Given  $f(1)$  and  $f(2)$ , we can easily find  $a$  and  $b$  such that  $f(1)=a+b$  and  $f(2)=2a+\tfrac b2$ . Shift down to give  $f(1)=f(2)=0$ . We will show that  $f\equiv 0$ . $P(2,2)$  gives   $$ \frac52f(2)=f(4)+f(1)\implies f(4)=0. $$  Now,  $P(2x,2)$  and  $P(x,1)$  give   $$ f(4x)=-f\left(\frac1x\right)=f(x) $$  for all  $x$ , so  $P(2,2x)$  gives   $$ \frac52f(2x)=f(4x)+f(x)=2f(x), $$  and thus  $f(2x)=\tfrac45f(x)$  and  $f(x)=f(4x)=\tfrac{16}{25}f(x)$ , which immediately yields  $f\equiv 0$ , as desired.  $\square$

The answer is  $f(x) = \lambda_1 x + \lambda_2 x ^{-1}$  for any real constants  $\lambda_1$  and  $\lambda_2$ . Indeed,  $f(x) \equiv x$  and  $f(x) \equiv 1/x$  work and the set of solutions is an  ${\mathbb R}$ -vector space.

To prove they are the only ones, we may by shifting assume that \[ f(1) = f(2) = 0 \] and try to show  $f$  is the zero function.

Let  $P(x,y)$  denote the given assertion. First, note that  $P(x,x)$  gives we get \[ f(x^2) = (x+1/x) f(x) \qquad \forall x. \] By replacing  $xy$  and  $y/x$  with  $a^2$  and  $b^2$  in the given we get the more symmetric (and square-free) assertion \begin{align*} 	Q(a,b) : \qquad 	\left( \frac ab + \frac ba \right) f(ab) 	&= f(a^2) + f(b^2)  	&= \left( a+\frac1a \right) f(a) 	+ \left( b+\frac1b \right) f(b). \end{align*} The idea is to now compute  $f(4x)$  in terms of  $f(x)$  in two different ways: because the way the equations are linear, we should get some constant multiple. To begin  $Q(2,2) \implies f(4) = 0$ . Next, for any  $x > 0$ , note that \begin{align*} 	Q(x,4) \implies 		\left( \frac x4 + \frac 4x \right) f(4x) 		&= \left( x + \frac 1x  \right) f(x) 		 	Q(x,2) \implies 		\left( \frac x2 + \frac 2x \right) f(2x) 		&= \left( x+\frac1x \right) f(x) 		 	Q(2x,2) \implies 		\left( x + \frac 1x \right) f(4x) 		&= \left( 2x+\frac1{2x} \right) f(2x) 		= \left( 2x + \frac{1}{2x} \right) 		\left( x+ \frac 1x \right) f(x). \end{align*} Thus  $f(4x)$  is a multiple of  $f(x)$  in two different ways! If  $f(x) \neq 0$ , then we would have to have \[ 	2x + \frac{1}{2x} 	= \left( x + \frac{1}{x} \right) 	\left( \frac x4 + \frac 4x \right) 	= \frac{x^2}{4} + \frac{4}{x^2} + \frac{17}{4}. \] But by AM-GM  $\frac{x^2}{4} + 4 \ge 2x$ , and  $\frac{4}{x^2} + \frac 14 \ge \frac{2}{x} > \frac{1}{2x}$ , so this is a contradiction.
